articles.title: Bruce Springsteen’s youngest son, Sam, grew up with a rock legend for a dad, but followed a different dream and became a Jersey City firefighter
articles.summary: When your father is one of the biggest names in rock music, it's easy to imagine the family legacy being centered around guitar and a stage.
articles.body: When your father is one of the biggest names in rock music, it's easy to imagine the family legacy being centered around guitar and a stage. But not every child of a star follows the spotlight; some chase their own path into adulthood.For Bruce Springsteen and his wife, Patti Scialfa, it was all about being proud when their youngest son, Sam, chose a job that asks him to run toward danger when most people run away.Sam did not catapult to the path all at once; it grew slowly over years of training and hard work in small New Jersey townsBruce Springsteen's youngest son Sam becomes a Jersey City firefighter, and his mom's message says it allBruce Springsteen is often called the voice of New Jersey, and while most of us would expect that the next generations would also take up a similar path for their lives, his youngest son is serving the state in a very different way. His wife Patti Scialfa took to Instagram to congratulate their son Sam, who is 25, on becoming a firefighter in Jersey City.Scialfa posted teh congratulatory message with a short and heartfelt caption, “CONGRATULATIONS,” she wrote, adding a fire emoji. She continued: “You followed your dreams…JC firefighter .. 💪Stay safe 💪.. ❤️love your brave heart❤️.” The post came with a black-and-white photo of Sam. As per the report, family friend Rita Wilson commented: “Go Sam!!!!!”Sam had taken a civil service exam to join the department.According to USA Today, he sat the exam in March. He was already an experienced firefighter by then. Sam has worked as a volunteer with the Colts Neck, where the family has a home, followed by Long Branch and North Wildwood fire departments.His training began years earlier.In 2014, Scialfa shared a smiling photo of Sam in uniform after he graduated from the Monmouth County Fire Academy. “My youngest son, Sam, graduated from Monmouth County Fire Academy tonight,” she wrote, with the hashtag “our family hero.” Monmouth County Fire Marshal Henry Stryker III told USA Today at the time that Sam was “very smart”. He also said Sam “enjoyed what he was doing.”Also read: Billionaire Tyler Perry gave his family 60 days to find jobs or lose his financial support: Why he refused to keep funding their livesHis work has made a real difference tooIn 2016, while serving with the North Wildwood Fire Department, Sam and another firefighter worked together to rescue a fisherman stuck in the mud. The Cape May County Herald covered the rescue.Sam grew up in a famous household, but his parents say music was never forced on their children. Bruce and Patti also have son Evan, who was 29 at the time of the report, and daughter Jessica, 27. In a 2017 interview with The New York Times, Bruce said, “We had our kids late, I was 40 when our first son was born, and they showed a healthy disinterest in our work over all the years”.He added, “They had their own musical heroes; they had their own music they were interested in. They’d be pretty blank-faced if someone mentioned a song title of mine.” He also said, “I kind of like that... I always looked upon that as that we did a good job.”Also Read: Zach Bryan reveals how his mother's alcoholism changed her from the woman he loved into someone he feared, and how he eventually forgave her: In an interview with Matthew McConaughey, he opens up about childhood abuse, loss and the road to understanding addictionYou use AI every day. articles.title: “My mother asked us to leave and we moved out with nothing!”: How a journalist couple turned job loss and despair into Patrakar Vada Pav, selling 100+ vada pavs daily and fulfilling bulk orders
articles.summary: Jasveer Singh Jassi and his wife, Sudha Kumari Sahu, run a vada pav cart in Noida.
articles.body: Jasveer Singh Jassi and his wife, Sudha Kumari Sahu, run a vada pav cart in Noida. There are no news bulletins to prepare, no television studios to walk into and no newsroom deadlines to meet. Instead, their days revolve around preparing food, serving customers and ensuring that the business keeps running.For a couple who spent years working in the media, this was not easy and definitely not the life they had imagined. Jassi had worked with several regional and national television networks over nearly 12 years, while Sudha had built a career spanning around seven years. Together, they had imagined a future in which their education, professional experience and earnings would provide stability.But life had other plans.When their media careers came to an abrupt halt in 2022, the couple found themselves struggling to pay rent and meet everyday expenses. Their savings dwindled, and the prospect of finding another job in the same industry offered little immediate relief. What followed was a journey through a tiffin service, a food cart, difficult family circumstances and the challenge of rebuilding their lives without financial support.“We have no regrets about what we are doing,” he says. “We work extremely hard, earn our daily bread ourselves and live on what we earn. That is what matters to us.” To understand how a journalist arrived at this point, one has to go back to 2018, when an ordinary afternoon at home changed the way Jassi looked at the world.2018: The moment that changed how he saw charityJassi grew up in a financially modest family in Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh. His work in the media eventually brought him to Noida, where he settled because it was close to his workplace. In 2018, while he was getting ready for work, he witnessed a small incident. My mother was giving away old clothes in exchange for household items. A middle-aged man accompanied by a young child came and asked for clothes, my mother picked up a few and gave him. While the vendors were haggling for 'good' clothes, this man who actually needed it had no choice. I asked the vendors to go away and asked the man to choose from the lot. He could have taken as much as he wanted, but he chose only three pieces. That really shook me,” Jassi recalls.“What struck me was his self-respect. He needed the clothes, yet he was not willing to take everything simply because it was available."Jassi began questioning the way people treated their surplus possessions. Clothes that had become old, ill-fitting or unwanted in one household could be valuable to someone else. Until then, he had seen the process of giving away old clothes as a routine household activity. That day, he began to see it differently. He asked his mother to set aside clothes for him instead of distributing them through the usual channels. He would decide where they went and who received them. The following day, he began a social initiative called Patrakar Ki Potli. The name was inspired by the traditional potli, a bundle used to carry clothes, food and other essentials while travelling. “I wanted to change the way we looked at things we no longer needed,” he says. “Something that is useless or extra for one person could be something another person has never had the opportunity to own.”He began taking clothes to underprivileged communities and slum settlements whenever his work schedule allowed. He also started sharing his efforts on social media. Gradually, friends, neighbours, colleagues and acquaintances began contributing. Some gave clothes, while others donated stationery, household items and other useful materials. The initiative continued to grow, bringing Jassi into contact with people whose lives were very different from his own.Beyond clothes: A social worker's expanding missionPatrakar Ki Potli was only the beginning. As Jassi became more involved in social work, he began exploring other causes that needed attention. His work expanded to include support for organ donation awareness and the LGBTQ+ community. His interest in the latter stemmed from a simple question: what if his own child were born into a community that society routinely misunderstood or discriminated against? "I kept thinking that when I eventually had a child, I would have no control over who that child became. That is nature's decision. Yet I saw how much hatred and fear people directed towards transgender people,” he says. “I wanted people to look at them differentlynot with pity, not with sympathy, but with an open mind. I wanted society to understand them as people who deserve the same respect as everyone else.”Another initiative emerged from his interactions with people living in orphanages, old-age homes and homes for widows. Jassi began wondering why these institutions, which often housed people experiencing different forms of loneliness and social exclusion, could not be brought together. He approached the organisers of the institutions and created an opportunity for their residents to meet and interact. Children from orphanages could spend time with elderly residents, while widows and other residents could find companionship and a sense of belonging. The idea was to help people who had lost or lacked family connections form new relationships.A wedding that challenged conventionJassi had also begun speaking out against dowry, albeit on a small scale. He believed that marriage should not be a financial transaction, but putting that belief into practice would require more than public statements. In 2020, he married Sudha Kumari Sahu, who originally hails from Kolkata and had worked in print and electronic media. The two had discussed their values before marriage, including their opposition to dowry and the social expectations surrounding weddings. Sudha understood what Jassi wanted to do.“We are young, we are earning and we have a voice,” Jassi recalls telling her. “If we want society to change, we cannot keep waiting for somebody else to do it. We have to begin with ourselves.” Together, they decided that their wedding would carry a message. They called it Ek Vivaah Aisa Bhi-a wedding with a difference.The couple decided to pay for the wedding from their own savings rather than depend on their parents. They would spend only what they could afford, without borrowing money or organising an elaborate ceremony to satisfy social expectations. Their wedding was deliberately simple. There was no elaborate mandap, no traditional rounds around the sacred fire, no grand procession and no expensive series of rituals. The ceremony lasted just four hours, from noon to 4 pm. Jassi bought his wedding outfit online, knowing he would probably never wear it again. Sudha purchased a lehenga for approximately ₹3,000 from her own savings. The food was equally simple- halwa, puri, subzi and water, served in the spirit of a community meal.But the most significant feature of the wedding was the guest list. Instead of filling the venue with relatives and acquaintances invited out of social obligation, the couple invited people from orphanages, old-age homes, homes for widows and communities they had supported through their social work.People who had once been recipients of assistance became the chief guests at their wedding. For Jassi, this was a way of recognising the people who had shaped his outlook on life. He also says the wedding invitation attracted attention beyond his immediate circle. According to him, Union Minister Nitin Gadkari's office contacted him after the invitation came to the minister's attention. Jassi recalls receiving the minister's wishes and later receiving a letter addressed to the couple.When the applause faded, life at home became difficultBut the admiration the couple received outside their home did not necessarily translate into acceptance within it. Jassi says that after the wedding, tensions began to surface over his social work, his priorities and the way he chose to live. He recalls being questioned about whether his activism could support a household financially.His family had concerns about his decision to devote time and energy to causes that did not generate an income. As disagreements grew, he felt that his wife was also being treated unfairly. For Jassi, the issue became one of dignity and equality. He recalls confronting his mother over the way women in the household were treated.“If one woman deserves respect, then every woman deserves respect,” he says, recalling his argument. “I told my mother that as you expect and deserve respect, so does my wife. Respect cannot be reserved for one person while the others are humiliated.”His remarks, he says, were not well received. He recalls his mother telling him, in effect, that he had yet to prove himself independently. “Let us see how far you get,” she told him, according to Jassi. “You are still living within these four walls. You do not pay the rent, electricity, water or grocery bills. You think earning a little money and getting married makes you independent?” The exchange exposed a larger conflict between Jassi's ideals and the expectations of his family.He says he did not want to continue living in an environment where disagreements were turning into daily confrontations. He and Sudha understood that they can no longer live here with so much humiliation and left home without carrying a thing.June 2022: Two media careers come to a halt"We moved out of our house with practically nothing. We had no home for 3-4 days, and gradully found a rented apartment and built a home with all our savings and while we were barely surviving, our media careers came to an end."Jassi had spent nearly 12 years in journalism, working with several regional and national news networks, including India Today Network, Zee News Haryana, Khabar India, Khabar Hindustan, Sadhna MP-CG, TV100, HBN 24x7 and ETV. Sudha had also spent years building her career in the media. But around April 2022, Sudha lost her job. Jassi's salary was subsequently cut substantially, leaving the couple struggling to meet their expenses. By around June, they were confronting the reality that their combined income could no longer sustain their lifestyle.They had been living in Noida, in a rented home and had planned their expenses around their salaries. Their earnings went towards rent, food, utilities and everyday living costs. Jassi also had an EMI on a Bullet motorcycle he had purchased before marriage. When Sudha lost her job, the financial strain increased. Jassi tried to find other opportunities while continuing at his workplace, but his reduced salary was eventually insufficient to cover even the rent.Sudha later found work in a channel, but it also shut down, leaving her unemployed again. The couple had little financial cushion to fall back on. They were educated, experienced professionals, but their immediate priority was no longer a newsroom position or career progression. It was survival.“We were earning and spending according to what we made. We had no big financial backup,” Jassi says. “When the jobs went, everything became uncertain. We had to think about how we would pay the rent and feed ourselves.” They tried to find jobs, but the uncertainty continued. Eventually, they realised they could not keep waiting for the media industry to provide a solution. One night, they decided to start again. Their first thought was to turn to something they could do themselves, without expensive training, a major investment or a long period without income.The answer, they hoped, lay in food.The tiffin service: 70 meals on the first dayJassi and Sudha knew how to prepare basic meals for themselves, but running a food business was a different challenge. They had no formal training in the restaurant industry, no established business infrastructure and little money to experiment with.They decided to start a tiffin service called Patrakar Couple Tiffin Service.During the monsoon of 2022, they began preparing for the venture. They bought tiffin containers, organised the necessary supplies and put up a flex sign outside their home to attract customers. They announced the launch in advance, hoping to build enough interest to make the effort worthwhile. On the first day, they delivered 70 tiffins, priced at ₹70 each. For the couple, it was an overwhelming moment.“We cried with happiness,” Jassi recalls. “We had been running around looking for jobs, wondering what would happen to us. Then, on the first day, we served 70 tiffins. We felt that perhaps we had finally found a way forward.”The couple continued the service for roughly a year, until 2023.But the business demanded consistency. Customers depended on them for daily meals, and every order came with a commitment that had to be honoured. Finding reliable domestic help proved difficult. Jassi says they changed helpers repeatedly, around 36 times over the course of a year, by his estimate. The work fell heavily on Sudha, and the couple found themselves struggling to balance the physical demands of the business with the responsibilities of running a household. They had wanted to build a sustainable livelihood, but the daily pressure was becoming difficult to manage.The tiffin service had shown them that customers were willing to pay for their work. What they needed now was a business model they could run with fewer logistical complications. That was when they turned to vada pav.73 vada pavs and a new beginningThe couple visited Shridih and Siddhivinayak and it was from there that they got the inspirtaion of selling Vada Pav. They came home, experimented and perfected the recipe and began their work. On their first day, they prepared 73 vada pavs. All 73 sold within roughly an hour to an hour and 15 minutes.For Jassi, it was another moment of relief.“Every single one sold. We were so happy. I remember thinking that this was something we could do. My wife would not have to carry the entire burden of the tiffin service. I could handle the cart and the sales, and we could work together without putting her through the same struggle.” But the initial success was followed by another challenge.When they returned to set up the cart, other vendors objected. According to Jassi, complaints were made to the local market committee, and he had to spend around three hours negotiating and trying to secure permission to operate.The couple arrived at around 4 pm, but the cart was not ready to begin serving until approximately 7.30 pm.Jassi says his experience as a journalist proved useful. Years of speaking to people, handling difficult conversations and navigating tense situations had taught him how to communicate without escalating a disagreement.“I used what journalism had taught me, how to talk to people, how to handle a difficult situation and how to keep my composure,” he says. “I knew that if I gave up that day, it would become even harder to return the next day.” While he tried to resolve the dispute, Sudha remained at the cart. Jassi recalls that she was pregnant at the time, making the physical demands and uncertainty of the situation particularly difficult.Eventually, they managed to begin selling. The experience reinforced their determination to continue. They had already lost their jobs and abandoned one business model. They could not afford to let another obstacle push them back to square one. Their food cart became more than a source of income. It was a way to retain control over their lives at a time when so much else had slipped beyond their control.No regrets, but a painful question of dignityAsk Jassi whether he regrets leaving behind a career in journalism, and his answer is immediate: neither he nor Sudha regrets the decision to pursue their own livelihood. But he acknowledges the emotional cost.He believes their families, who had once been proud of their professional identities and their unconventional wedding, now feel embarrassed by the sight of them selling food from a cart. He says that when people ask about their work, relatives sometimes downplay what they do or describe it as a temporary arrangement.For Jassi, that hurts—not because he considers the work beneath him, but because he feels his family struggles to see the dignity in it.“We may have brought embarrassment to our families in their eyes,” he says. “We were educated, we worked in television, we were part of what people call VIP culture. Now we sell vada pav, run a tiffin service and do whatever work is necessary to earn our living.” He pauses before adding that the couple's choice is not about proving anything to anyone. “We earn our own money, feed ourselves and work extremely hard. Why should we be ashamed of that? We are not asking anyone to support us. We are trying to stand on our own feet.”For Jassi, the contrast is especially painful because his social work and their wedding had once attracted admiration. The same people who appreciated their values may now find it difficult to accept the form their lives have taken.Yet he remains unwilling to measure success only through a job title, a salary or the approval of relatives.Their story is still unfolding. The couple have had to learn a new trade, navigate uncertain earnings and confront the realities of running a small food business. They have also had to redefine what independence means when professional credentials do not guarantee financial security.What remains constant is their determination to keep working.A different definition of successJassi's journey began with three pieces of clothing selected by a man who needed them but refused to take more than he considered necessary. That encounter led him to question how society treats people who have less. Years later, he and Sudha found themselves on the other side of that question, confronting a society that often measures people by their occupations and earnings.They had once used their professional platforms to draw attention to the lives of others. Now, they are trying to build a life of their own through work that many people might consider a step down from their former careers. For Jassi, however, there is no shame in the work itself.He and Sudha have already demonstrated that they are willing to question convention: through their social initiatives, a wedding that rejected dowry and extravagance, and the decision to leave a difficult household situation rather than continue fighting.Losing their jobs forced them to question another conventionthat education and professional experience should lead to a particular kind of life, and that anything outside it represents failure.Their vada pav cart may not offer the security or status of a television newsroom. But it gives them a way to earn, to work together and to keep moving forward. Perhaps the most telling part of Jassi's story is that he does not ask for sympathy. He asks, instead, that people recognise the effort behind what he and his wife do.For a couple who have had to rebuild their lives more than once, that recognition may matter as much as the money they earn. And as they continue serving customers in Noida, one vada pav at a time, they are making their own argument about dignity: a person's worth is not determined by where they work, but by the honesty with which they do their work and the courage it takes to begin again.You use AI every day. articles.title: Former Delhi HR professional quits her corporate job and moves to Goa in search of purpose but faces financial worries and uncertainty in her new life
articles.summary: Quitting a stable job may seem like a dream come true, offering freedom from office routines, fixed schedules and daily responsibilities.
articles.body: Quitting a stable job may seem like a dream come true, offering freedom from office routines, fixed schedules and daily responsibilities. But starting over is not always as easy as it appears. As the initial excitement settles, concerns about finances, future plans and finding the right direction can begin to surface, making the new life feel just as uncertain as the one left behind.For Arpita Sahu, a former human resources professional who worked in Delhi, these questions have become part of her move to Goa. After completing her MBA and spending four and a half years working, she decided to step away from corporate life and begin again in a new place. Through videos shared on Instagram, Sahu has been documenting the emotional side of this transition, from the hope of finding a place to call home to the anxiety of living without a regular salary. Her experience offers a glimpse into a side of career change that is often missing from pictures of scenic beaches and carefree living.A new address, but no ready-made answersSahu's move to Goa was not simply about exchanging a busy city for a holiday destination. She was looking for a fresh chapter and hoping to discover what she wanted from life beyond her established career. Her professional background includes experience as an HR professional at companies such as Info Edge India Ltd and Cognizant, according to the details shared about her LinkedIn profile. Leaving that world behind meant giving up the familiarity of a structured working life and stepping into an uncertain future.In a video documenting her arrival, Sahu showed herself packing her belongings and leaving her corporate routine behind. The decision marked a change in more than her location. She was also entering a phase in which her next steps were not already mapped out by a job, an office schedule or familiar professional expectations.She expressed hope that Goa would eventually feel like home and that she would find people with whom she could connect. Until then, she said, she would continue searching for that sense of belonging. The uncertainty is central to her story. Moving somewhere new can offer the possibility of reinvention, but it does not automatically provide a community, a sense of direction or answers to questions that may have existed long before the move.The first Monday without an officeThe reality of leaving work became particularly clear when Sahu experienced her first Monday without the usual expectation of going to the office. For many employees, Monday represents the beginning of another working week. For someone who has left a job voluntarily, however, the same day can bring an unfamiliar mix of relief, freedom and unease. The routine may be gone, but the questions about what to do next remain. Sahu spoke openly about the pressure she felt during this period. She was conscious of the money in her bank account and knew that her savings would not last indefinitely. Without a regular salary, everyday decisions could carry a different weight.She also described struggling with her attention span, saying she found herself repeatedly checking Instagram and looking at follower numbers instead of watching something without distraction. Her experience highlights how a major life change can affect more than finances. A job provides not only income but also structure, regular goals and a sense of progress. Once that framework disappears, a person may have to build a new routine while managing the uncertainty that comes with it.When freedom comes with financial pressureSahu's account challenges the idea that leaving a corporate job automatically leads to a happier or more meaningful life. The decision may create room to explore new interests, but it can also introduce pressure to prove that the choice was worthwhile. She described an unspoken expectation to do well, alongside the knowledge that her financial resources were limited. That combination can make a fresh start emotionally demanding, particularly when there is no clear timeline for finding work, building a new career or deciding what comes next.Social media can add another layer to this experience. Platforms make it easy to document a move, share personal reflections and connect with people going through similar changes. At the same time, checking views, followers and engagement can become a distraction when someone is already trying to work out their next steps. Sahu's willingness to share these concerns makes her story more relatable than a simple account of quitting a job and moving to a scenic location. It shows that uncertainty does not necessarily disappear when a person makes a bold decision. Sometimes, it becomes more visible.Searching for a life that feels like homeThe response to Sahu's videos reflected different ideas about what makes a life fulfilling. Some users encouraged her to consider whether Goa's slower pace would support her goals, while others shared broader reflections on living in the present rather than organising life entirely around future achievements. One commenter suggested that Mumbai might offer a faster pace and better opportunities for stability. Another encouraged her to focus on experiencing life as it unfolds rather than feeling compelled to achieve a particular purpose.These reactions point to a question without a universal answer: should people prioritise financial security, professional growth, personal freedom or the search for a place where they feel they belong? Sahu's experience does not establish that leaving a job is the right choice for everyone, nor does it suggest that moving to Goa will resolve every concern. Instead, it shows the complexity of making a major change without knowing exactly how the next chapter will unfold.For now, her journey is still in progress. She is adjusting to a new city, confronting financial concerns and looking for a sense of purpose and connection. The move may eventually lead her towards the life she wants, but the process is unlikely to be as straightforward as a change of address. Perhaps the most revealing part of her story is not that she walked away from a corporate career. It is that she is willing to acknowledge what comes after the decision: the doubts, the pressure and the difficult work of building a life when the familiar roadmap is no longer there.You use AI every day. articles.title: Influencer with 1.3 million followers dies by suicide in Chennai; father alleges cyberbullying
articles.summary: CHENNAI: A 27-year-old financial consultant and social media influencer died by suicide after alleged cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and
articles.body: CHENNAI: A 27-year-old financial consultant and social media influencer died by suicide after alleged cyberbullying, defamatory social media posts and repeated blocking of his online channels. V Harish, who had 1.3 million followers on social media, was found hanging in his rented villa at Muttukadu, Chennai, on Tuesday. He had been posting content on finance and investments for the past five years.Police said his online channel was mass-reported and blocked in September, along with another social media account. He launched a new channel, which was also reported and blocked.Harish’s father J Vinayagam lodged a complaint with police alleging that Jason Samuel, another influencer, had subjected his son to sustained cyberbullying, defamatory posts and threats, causing severe mental distress. According to the complaint, Samuel published videos and posts on Oct 18 accusing Harish of being a fraud and misleading the public.Vinayagam Harish recorded a video before his death, saying Samuel was responsible for his decision. In the video, Harish reportedly claimed that Samuel had threatened to get all his social media accounts blocked and prevent him from creating new ones.Samuel denied the allegations in a social media post. He said he had questioned Harish’s credentials and authorisation to provide financial advice. Harish did not have SEBI’s registered investment adviser (RIA) licence and had misrepresented his registration with Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), Samuel said, adding he never expected Harish to take such an extreme step.Vinayagam has asked police to examine the video recorded by his son before his death, preserve relevant digital evidence and investigate the circumstances surrounding the blocking of Harish’s accounts.Kanathur police have registered a case of unnatural death and are looking at statements of both the sides.(Assistance for those having suicidal thoughts is available on TN’s health helpline 104 and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050.)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Chennai | Silver Rate in Chennai | Bank Holidays in Chennai | Public Holidays in Chennai | Chennai AQI | Weather in Chennai | Petrol Price in Chennai | Diesel Price in Chennai | CNG Price in Chennai | LPG Price in ChennaiStay updated with the latest Chennai news. articles.title: 'Multiple cut marks, throats slit': Mother, lover, son kill 13-year-old twins who opposed her relationship
articles.summary: Mother and son, along with her partner, held for alleged murder of 13-year-old twins in Deeg’s Badesra village, Alwar; police cite motive as relationship dispute.
articles.body: ALWAR: Two 13-year-old twin brothers were found murdered in Badesra village of Deeg district Tuesday morning, with police alleging their widowed mother conspired with her paramour to kill them because the boys opposed the relationship.The victims, identified as Vinay and Vishnu Chaudhary, were discovered dead in a plot near their house around 6am. Their maternal aunt had raised the alarm when the twins failed to return after leaving home early Tuesday, following which a search was launched.Deeg superintendent of police Kambale Sharan Gopinath said the twins’ throats had been slit and injuries inflicted on their heads. Police said both bodies bore multiple cut marks and head injuries.According to investigators, the mother, Preeti, called her paramour to the house, where he and her 16-year-old elder son carried out the killings at her behest. All three were taken into custody and are being questioned.Investigators claimed the twins had become an “obstacle” to the mother’s relationship with her paramour – a resident of the same village – while their elder brother supported their mother.Police said Preeti was married to her now-deceased husband Niranjan Singh, a resident of Saroth Mansa village in Hathras district of Uttar Pradesh, 20 years ago. The couple had four children – an 18-year-old daughter, a 16-year-old son, and the 13-year-old twin brothers.Preeti and her four children had moved to her parental home in Badesra after Singh’s death several years ago.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Jaipur | Silver Rate in Jaipur | Bank Holidays in Jaipur | Public Holidays in Jaipur | Jaipur AQI | Weather in Jaipur | Petrol Price in Jaipur | Diesel Price in Jaipur | CNG Price in Jaipur | LPG Price in JaipurStay updated with the latest Jaipur news. articles.summary: Empresas ganham espaço em setores como eletrônicos, robótica e veículos elétricos, pressionando concorrentes e alimentando disputas comerciais e preocupações com segurança.
articles.body:

Não faz muito tempo, a GoPro era sinônimo de câmera de ação. Em seu auge, em 2015, a empresa americana reinava absoluta, com cerca de 6,6 milhões de unidades vendidas naquele ano e participação de mercado superior a 70%.

Hoje, a pioneira luta pela própria sobrevivência. O principal culpado? A concorrência chinesa.

As maiores rivais da GoPro, DJI e Insta360, entraram no mercado de câmeras de ação em 2019 e 2021, respectivamente. Hoje, elas respondem por mais de 90% das vendas globais de câmeras inteligentes portáteis.

Alexander Hannemann, que usa regularmente câmeras de ação para filmar seus passeios demotocicleta, diz que trocou a GoPro pela Insta360 há cerca de dois anos.

"A qualidade é muito melhor do que a da GoPro, mesmo quando estou acelerando e entrando em curvas a cerca de 80 quilômetros por hora", disse à DW.

A GoPro escapou da falência em setembro, após baque por apostas malsucedidas em produtos e concorrência dos smartphones — Foto: Christian Ohde/imageBROKER/picture alliance via DW

A crescente liderança tecnológica da China

O caso da GoPro não é exceção. Desde aproximadamente 2010, muitas marcas chinesas não apenas alcançaram, mas superaram rivais ocidentais que antes dominavam o setor de tecnologia de consumo, de TVs inteligentes a aspiradores robóticos.

Já ficou para trás a época em que Made in China era sinônimo de produtos baratos e produzidos em massa.

"A China ainda fabrica produtos acessíveis", afirma Chris Pereira, empreendedor canadense e autor com mais de 20 anos de experiência no país. "Mas os produtos também são de alta qualidade."

Essa combinação fez com que bem mais da metade dos novos produtos globais de tecnologia para o consumidor passassem a vir de fornecedores chineses, acrescenta Pereira.

BYD , Xpeng e outras montadoras chinesas venderam quase dois terços de todos os carros elétricos comercializados no ano passado, superando empresas já estabelecidas, como a Tesla.

No segmento de aspiradores robóticos, marcas chinesas dominam o mercado global, enquanto a americana iRobot, antiga pioneira do setor, tem dificuldades para competir.

Mas por que as empresas chinesas superam cada vez mais seus rivais ocidentais?

Pereira, cuja consultoria iMpact ajuda empresas chinesas a ganhar espaço no exterior, atribui esse sucesso à intensa concorrência doméstica em cidades como Shenzhen, Hangzhou e Xangai, a cadeias de suprimentos altamente integradas e a uma cultura empresarial orientada para a ação, que permite às companhias inovar e responder rapidamente aos problemas.

Outros fatores importantes para a vantagem competitiva chinesa incluem automação industrial incomparável, uso estratégico de inteligência artificial na manufatura, agilidade regulatória e mão de obra relativamente barata.

Juntos, esses elementos resultam em custos de produção significativamente menores e ciclos de inovação muito mais rápidos do que os observados em outras economias.

Joey Cheng, fundador da Prolo Ring, empresa que fabrica anéis que permitem acesso a controles remotos e outros dispositivos usando apenas os polegares — Foto: Benjamin Bathke/DW

Joey Cheng, que se mudou para os Estados Unidos para fazer doutorado há mais de 20 anos, conhece tanto o lado do consumidor americano quanto o do produtor chinês.

Embora sua startup esteja sediada nos EUA, quase toda a produção é realizada em Shenzhen, onde é fabricada uma grande parcela dos equipamentos eletrônicos e dispositivos de consumo do mundo.

"A cadeia de suprimentos de Shenzhen é praticamente inevitável para reduzir custos e desenvolver produtos rapidamente", diz Cheng. "Especialmente para uma startup, é preciso colocar o produto no mercado depressa ou você será atropelado pela concorrência."

Persistem preocupações com privacidade e segurança

Embora os consumidores estejam aderindo em massa às empresas chinesas, algumas ressalvas permanecem.

Uma pesquisa recente mostrou que mais de 90% dos europeus não confiam seus dados a empresas chinesas de tecnologia, enquanto cerca de 80% desconfiam das americanas. Os alemães apresentaram o nível mais elevado de desconfiança.

Embora utilize câmeras da DJI e da Insta360 em suas viagens, a blogueira Nadine diz que prefere não ter dispositivos domésticos conectados de fabricantes asiáticos."

"Meu aspirador robô é de uma empresa alemã justamente por isso: para que os dados permaneçam em conformidade com as regulamentações alemãs. Afinal, os fabricantes podem se conectar diretamente à câmera", disse ela, referindo-se a casos de invasão de câmeras e sistemas de áudio envolvendo aspiradores robóticos.

A fabricante chinesa de óculos inteligentes Xreal entrou recentemente no mercado europeu por meio de varejistas, como a britânica Currys — Foto: Andy Wong/AP Photo/picture alliance via DW

Ainda assim, Pereira afirma que empresas chinesas em expansão internacional precisam pagar um "prêmio de confiança".

"Esse déficit de confiança significa que elas precisam ser ainda mais competitivas em produto e preço para que o mercado as escolha", afirma.

Segundo ele, essa distância pode ser reduzida por meio de uma presença física nos mercados estrangeiros, como a primeira fábrica europeia de carros de passeio da BYD , cuja inauguração é esperada para o fim deste ano na Hungria.

Empresas chinesas afirmam cumprir as regras de proteção de dados da União Europeia. No entanto, leis de segurança nacional tanto nos EUA quanto na China podem obrigar companhias a entregar dados ao governo, e autoridades alemãs observam que há supervisão limitada sobre possíveis transferências de dados de servidores europeus para outros países.

Além das preocupações com privacidade, empresas chinesas de tecnologia de consumo também vêm sendo alvo de escrutínio por suspeitas de espionagem e outros riscos, mais recentemente em relação a dispositivos conectados, como veículos elétricos.

Uma nova guerra comercial está a caminho?

Diante das preocupações de segurança, dos déficits comerciais e do domínio chinês em diversos setores, os Estados Unidos e vários outros países ocidentais impuseram tarifas, listas de restrições e exigências rigorosas a importações e empresas chinesas.

No fim de julho, o governo Trump proibiu a importação de robôs humanoides fabricados fora dos EUA.

Um representante da fabricante chinesa de robôs Primebot disse à DW que todas as empresas chinesas de tecnologia de consumo estão sentindo os efeitos dessas medidas.

"Talvez busquemos cooperação com uma empresa americana local. Outra solução possível é construir uma fábrica lá", afirmou.

Países europeus e a própria União Europeia também avaliam a adoção de mais tarifas contra empresas chinesas.

Chris Pereira prevê que essas tarifas irão acelerar duas tendências entre as companhias chinesas: transferir mais produção para outros países e concentrar-se cada vez mais em desafiar marcas ocidentais de primeira linha com produtos premium.

"Autoridades e empresas chinesas reconhecem que a manufatura precisa ser localizada até certo ponto. Uma razão é amenizar as dificuldades de exportação; outra é gerar confiança local", resume Pereira.

"A outra tendência é que, uma vez que as tarifas eliminam a vantagem de preço na base do mercado, a margem que sobra está no topo. Por isso, marcas chinesas competem cada vez mais diretamente com nomes ocidentais já consolidados, justamente onde a confiança é mais importante."

As empresas ocidentais conseguem competir?

À medida que o domínio chinês continua crescendo, empresas ocidentais buscam formas de permanecer competitivas.

Kaz Merchant, que trabalha em uma companhia britânica de importação e exportação de equipamentos de tecnologia da informação, afirma que empresas menores, em particular, precisam encontrar nichos geográficos específicos.

"Elas precisam ter um diferencial próprio para determinado produto, algo que a China talvez não ofereça naquela região. Ou então precisam se associar a uma empresa chinesa", diz.

Para Pereira, uma questão fundamental que a Europa precisa resolver é a velocidade de resposta dos órgãos reguladores.

"Os reguladores chineses dizem de forma muito clara e rápida o que é possível fazer. Essa velocidade ajuda as empresas a se aperfeiçoar e ter sucesso no exterior", afirma.

"Se você esperar semanas por uma resposta, vai perder negócios."

articles.standfirst: Em 133 delas, mais próximas, amostras de sangue das aves devem ser coletadas para análises. Granja comercial de perus em Nova Itaberaba, no Oeste, teve foco confirmado, mas sem animais doentes.
articles.summary: Em 133 delas, mais próximas, amostras de sangue das aves devem ser coletadas para análises.
articles.body:
Uma operação da Companhia Integrada de Desenvolvimento Agrícola de Santa Catarina (Cidasc) fará visitas a cerca de 1,6 mil propriedades no entorno da granja onde foi confirmado o foco da doença de Newcastle . Em pouco mais de 130 delas , poderá ser necessária a coleta de amostras de sangue das aves para análises laboratoriais, conforme os critérios de vigilância sanitária.

O vírus da doença foi encontrado em uma granja comercial de perus de Nova Itaberaba , no Oeste do estado. Apesar da presença do micro-organismo, as aves não ficaram doentes.

🐔A doença de Newcastle é uma enfermidade viral que contamina aves domésticas e silvestres, podendo ser letal para esses animais. Em humanos, ela pode causar, no máximo, conjuntivite transitória, que costuma durar cerca de uma semana. A transmissão ocorre pelo contato, e não pelo consumo.

As equipes atuam diretamente na propriedade afetada e em um raio de 10 quilômetros ao redor do foco, com medidas para evitar a disseminação da doença e proteger a produção avícola do estado.

Coleta de sangue em ave de Santa Catarina — Foto: Cidasc/Divulgação

A granja onde o foco foi confirmado permanece interditada , com acesso restrito exclusivamente às equipes autorizadas da Cidasc e do Ministério da Agricultura e Pecuária (Mapa). As próximas etapas de trabalho no local são:

descarte adequado de equipamentos e materiais que tiveram contato com os animais

Granja em Nova Itaberaba onde foi confirmado foco da doença de Newcastle — Foto: Francieli de Moraes/NSC TV

A Cidasc destacou que o consumo de carne de aves e ovos de estabelecimentos inspecionados pelo Serviço Veterinário Oficial permanece seguro para a população.

Estes produtos podem ser identificados pela presença na embalagem de um dos selos de inspeção sanitária:

SIM - de um Serviço de Inspeção Municipal

Três países suspenderam importação de carne de frango de SC

Chile - suspensão das importações apenas de Santa Catarina

China - 14 estabelecimentos em Santa Catarina que exportam frango para China tiveram a comercialização com o país asiático suspensa. No Brasil, são 61 ao todo que comercializam o produto com os chineses

México - suspensão das compras de todo o Brasil

A Associação Brasileira de Proteína Animal (ABPA) afirmou que ainda não é possível estimar os possíveis impactos dessas suspensões nas exportações catarinenses.

O g1 entrou em contato com a Secretaria de Estado da Agricultura e Pecuária para abordar o mesmo assunto e não havia obtido retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

articles.title: Rosto em calçada no interior de SP: o que você vê? | G1
articles.standfirst: Rachaduras, manchas no concreto e folhas secas em rua de Cândido Rodrigues mobilizaram orações em cidade de 3 mil habitantes. Enquanto fiéis veem face de Cristo, padre pondera que percepção é subjetiva.
articles.summary: A suposta imagem de Jesus em calçada de Cândido Rodrigues mobilizou orações e visitas de fiéis após manchas e rachaduras formarem um rosto humano no concreto.
articles.body:
A aposentada Carmen da Costa não escondeu a emoção ao caminhar até a Rua Brasília e olhar com atenção para o concreto do chão. Para ela, as marcas e manchas surgidas na calçada são mais do que um desenho casual.

“Foi isso para a gente, é Deus voltando para mostrar para a gente que temos que ser mais unidos. É uma graça muito grande que nós recebemos, sinceramente a gente fica assim muito emocionada”, afirmou.

A revelação no pavimento alterou a rotina de Cândido Rodrigues , município no interior de São Paulo com pouco mais de 3 mil habitantes.

Imagem de rosto em calçada de Cândido Rodrigues (SP) intriga moradores. — Foto: Thiago Aureliano/EPTV

O trecho em frente ao número 390 virou ponto de visitação e oração, levando as autoridades locais a isolar a área com fita de sinalização para preservar a marcação e organizar o fluxo de curiosos e fiéis. Na noite de terça-feira (20), moradores chegaram a se reunir no local para rezar um terço.

Na avaliação do sacerdote, os contornos no concreto formam traços aleatórios que lembram uma figura humana, mas a associação com a imagem de Jesus é subjetiva e ligada à cultura e crença individual.

“Aparentemente é um rosto humano, independente de qualquer coisa. Aparentemente é um rosto humano, mas não dá para dizer 'olha, é o rosto de fulano, o rosto de ciclano'”, disse o sacerdote.

Padre Sebastião explicou ainda que as representações conhecidas de Cristo variam de acordo com construções culturais.

“Se é o rosto de Jesus, vai da fé e da sensibilidade de cada um, porque ninguém sabe direito como foi o rosto de Jesus. (...) Jesus Cristo, vamos dizer assim, nós podemos encontrá-lo verdadeiramente na Eucaristia e também na pessoa dos nossos irmãos mais pobres”, destacou.

Foto tirada por moradora no momento em que viu rosto em calçada em Cândido Rodrigues (SP). — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A descoberta da imagem ocorreu na noite de domingo (18), por volta das 20h40. A embaladora de frutas Maria Rosa Querico contava que descia a rua a caminho da casa do pai quando parou para admirar o céu.

“Olhei a lua e do nada veio um clarão azul e refletiu naquele local. Quando eu olhei, eu já vi a face de Cristo”, contou.

Surpresa com o que presenciou, Maria Rosa registrou a foto na calçada e enviou a imagem para a irmã, a auxiliar de escritório Mina Benite.

“Ela mandou primeiro pra mim. Aí ela perguntou: 'O que você vê nessa foto?'. Eu falei: 'Ah, eu estou vendo o rosto de Cristo'”, relatou Mina.

Cândido Rodrigues, cidade de 3 mil habitantes na região de Ribeirão Preto (SP). — Foto: Thiago Aureliano/EPTV

Mina caminhou até o endereço para ver pessoalmente e confirmou ter visto a figura com clareza, destacando inclusive um detalhe que chamou a atenção dos moradores: folhas secas presas sobre o concreto que parecem compor uma coroa de espinhos.

Moradora de uma casa logo em frente, a cuidadora Roseli da Silva conta que jamais havia notado qualquer alteração no chão, apesar de passar por ali diariamente. Ela explica que para enxergar o desenho é necessário se posicionar a certa distância.

“Sim, você tem que ir bem, meio distante para você ver”, explicou Roseli, ressaltando que, de perto, o local aparenta conter apenas manchas e rachaduras comuns.

Segundo os relatos dos moradores, o endereço continua recebendo visitas diárias de idosos e crianças de Cândido Rodrigues e de municípios vizinhos, dividindo opiniões entre a curiosidade sobre o fenômeno óptico e a manifestação espontânea de fé popular.

articles.title: ES tem mais de 233 mil mulheres em busca de um 'sugar daddy' | G1
articles.standfirst: Dados de uma plataforma de relacionamentos também mostram que existem 43.247 'sugar daddies' e 11.604 'sugar mommies' cadastrados em busca de relacionamento com pessoas mais novas.
articles.summary: Dados de uma plataforma de relacionamentos mostram que há 43.247 sugar daddies e 11.604 sugar mommies, contra 233.656 e 73.501 sugar babies femininas e masculinos, respectivamente.
articles.body:
ES tem mais mulheres à procura de um daddy do que homens à procura de uma mommy — Foto: Pixabay/Divulgação

Levantamento feito por uma plataforma de relacionamentos revelou que, no Espírito Santo, existem 233.656 mulheres "babies" à procura de um "sugar daddy". Ao todo, 43.247 homens estão cadastrados no site e buscam uma parceira mais jovem para poder bancar.

Segundo os dados, divulgados pelo site MeuPatrocínio, são cinco mulheres jovens para cada daddy em solo capixaba . Ainda segundo o levantamento, a renda média desses homens que buscam uma parceira pelo site é de R$ 76 mil.

🔍Em inglês, sugar baby significa "bebê de açúcar". A expressão nasceu nos Estados Unidos, no início do século 20, para definir a relação entre um homem mais velho e rico, o daddy (pai em inglês), que banca uma mulher jovem, a baby.

A plataforma não é exclusiva para daddies. Ela também reúne mulheres que se identificam como "sugar mommies" (ou seja, mulheres mais velhas à procura de "novinhos" para se relacionar e bancar). No estado, são 11.604 usuárias cadastradas, segundo o levantamento.

Já os chamados "babies masculinos" (homens mais novos à procura de uma parceira mais velha para serem bancados) no Espírito Santo é de 73.501 pessoas.

De maneira geral, entre sugar daddies, sugar mommies e sugar babies femininas e masculinos, são 362.008 pessoas cadastradas na plataforma de relacionamento apenas no Espírito Santo . É como se a população de Colatina e Linhares inteira estivesse inscrita no site.

"Muitas vezes, esses homens não têm um traquejo social muito grande e, justamente por terem focado mais no trabalho, eles se veem sozinhos e numa situação onde eles não sabem como conhecer outras pessoas. Então, eles procuram o site para ajudar a ter uma vida amorosa", explicou Caio Bittencourt, especialista em comportamento afetivo.

O levantamento foi realizado com usuários de todo o Brasil, mas os dados apresentados nesta reportagem são um recorte apenas do Espírito Santo.

Ainda de acordo com a plataforma, as sugar babies têm idade média de 27 anos e, em sua maioria, são estudantes e empreendedoras. Já entre os sugar daddies, a idade média é de 39 anos, e predominam empresários e executivos de indústrias.

De acordo com Bittencourt, o perfil das mulheres babies surpreende. Nem sempre elas estão à procura somente de serem bancadas.

"No Espírito Santo, cada vez mais os empresários crescem e mais as mulheres se cansam de homens que não agregam na vida amorosa e financeira. Muitas das babies já têm um trabalho com salário alto, então elas procuram alguém que corresponda às suas expectativas".

*Este conteúdo foi produzido por Rafaela Gomes, residente do 29º Curso de Residência em Jornalismo da Rede Gazeta, sob orientação de Vitor Ferri.

articles.title: Mineradora australiana identifica alto teor de terras raras em novo projeto de exploração no Sul de MG | G1
articles.standfirst: Sondagem da Power Minerals encontrou concentração de 40,5% em amostra de 1,2 metro. Empresa pretende divulgar primeira estimativa de recursos minerais no início de 2027.
articles.summary: Sondagem da Power Minerals encontrou concentração de 40,5% em amostra de 1,2 metro. Empresa pretende divulgar primeira estimativa de recursos minerais no início de 2027.
articles.body:
A mineradora australiana Power Minerals anunciou que encontrou alto teor de terras raras em seu novo projeto de exploração no Morro do Ferro, em Poços de Caldas (MG). Uma amostra de 1,2 metro apresentou concentração de 40,5% de óxidos totais de terras raras (TREO).

O mesmo furo de sondagem, identificado como MFSR-057, registrou um intervalo contínuo de 111 metros, desde a superfície, com teor médio de 8,25% de TREO. Dentro desse trecho, foram identificados 51 metros com média de 15,42% e outros 15 metros com teor médio de 20,42%.

🔎 Terras raras são um conjunto de 17 elementos químicos estratégicos, fundamentais em tecnologias como carros elétricos, turbinas eólicas, celulares e equipamentos de defesa. Os óxidos totais de terras raras (TREO na sigla em inglês) representam a medida da concentração destes elementos.

Power Minerals encontra alto teor de terras raras em novo projeto de exploração no Sul de Minas — Foto: Power Minerals/Divulgação

Os resultados das pesquisas também apontam a presença de elementos terras raras magnéticos — neodímio, praseodímio, terbo e dispróseo — na concentração de 7,73%, o que representa até 20% do total de terras raras das amostras. Esses elementos têm aplicações industriais e são utilizados na fabricação de ímãs permanentes de alto desempenho, sendo os que têm maior valor de mercado.

O projeto do Morro do Ferro foi adquirido pela Power Minerals em abril de 2026 por R$ 80 milhões . Desde então, a mineradora realiza uma campanha de sondagem para confirmar e aprofundar os dados de pesquisas anteriores.

"A gente tem resultados excelentes, muito acima dos esperados. Essa nova perspectiva que se apresenta com os resultados de sondagem eleva a perspectiva de produção de terras raras, eleva o teor e também eleva o volume, porque não só são teores acima do esperado, mas também no intervalo de 120 metros de profundidade. As sondagens anteriores chegavam até 70, 80 metros nos teores mais profundos, então, isso é muito animador porque a gente tem tanto maior teor quanto maior volume e isso, por consequência, gera o maior potencial de produção de terras-raras no projeto", afirma o diretor de Novos Negócios da Power Minerals, Luiz Curado.

De acordo com o executivo da Power, os teores identificados podem permitir uma lavra de menor volume em comparação com depósitos de concentrações mais baixas. Segundo ele, isso poderia reduzir a quantidade de material movimentado, o consumo de água e a necessidade de equipamentos e insumos no processamento.

Grupo australiano define alvo de exploração no 'Morro do Ferro' com até 10,7 milhões de toneladas de terras raras em MG — Foto: Divulgação / Power Minerals

Primeira estimativa de recursos deve sair em 2027

A empresa ainda precisa concluir etapas de pesquisa para determinar a quantidade de minério e a distribuição dos elementos no depósito. Os dados divulgados são de exploração e não representam uma estimativa de recursos ou reservas minerais.

De acordo com Curado, a Power Minerals já apresentou um alvo de exploração (Exploration Target) de aproximadamente 9 milhões de toneladas, com teor de 8%. O indicador aponta uma perspectiva inicial de volume e concentração, mas não equivale a uma estimativa de recursos minerais certificada.

A expectativa da empresa é divulgar a primeira estimativa de recursos no início de 2027, seguindo o código JORC, padrão australiano utilizado para a divulgação de informações sobre exploração, recursos e reservas minerais.

Inicialmente, a pesquisa previa 4 mil metros de sondagem, com uma sonda em operação durante um turno. Com os novos resultados, a companhia pretende ampliar o programa para 8,5 mil metros, contratar uma terceira sonda e passar a trabalhar em dois turnos.

Segundo o representante da Power, a ampliação busca investigar a continuidade da mineralização tanto em profundidade quanto na extensão lateral do depósito.

A transformação do depósito em uma operação comercial ainda depende de uma série de etapas, entre elas a definição dos recursos minerais, os estudos de processamento, a avaliação econômica e o licenciamento ambiental.

O Brasil possui as maiores reservas de terras raras do mundo depois da China — Foto: Getty Images

Os novos resultados de sondagem representam um avanço no conhecimento geológico do Morro do Ferro, mas a viabilidade econômica da exploração ainda depende de uma série de etapas, entre elas a definição com maior precisão do tamanho do depósito, os estudos de processamento, a avaliação econômica e o licenciamento ambiental.

A expectativa é concluir um estudo de escopo até meados de 2027. A partir dele, a companhia pretende avançar para um estudo de pré-viabilidade, previsto para o fim do mesmo ano. A decisão de investimento para construir uma planta de processamento poderá ocorrer no fim de 2028, a depender dos resultados.

Por isso, a empresa desenvolve estudos de metalurgia e mineralurgia para avaliar como os elementos poderão ser separados e recuperados.

"Vai ser um processamento seguindo o melhor padrão de governança, de sustentabilidade. Um processamento que não gera barragem, um processamento ambientalmente adequado à região, com reutilização de água para que a gente consiga de fato agregar dentro da cadeia e não gerar incômodo dentro da comunidade de Poços de Caldas", afirmou Curado.

articles.title: An Ahmedabad family spent Rs 2.2 lakh buying clothes in Singapore after Air India left their luggage behind; 11 years later, consumer commission orders airline to pay Rs 2.5 lakh
articles.summary: AHMEDABAD: An Ahmedabad family spent Rs 2.2 lakh buying clothes and other essentials in Singapore after Air India allegedly left their luggage behind at
articles.body: AHMEDABAD: An Ahmedabad family spent Rs 2.2 lakh buying clothes and other essentials in Singapore after Air India allegedly left their luggage behind at Ahmedabad airport in January 2015.Eleven years later, a consumer commission has ordered the airline to reimburse Rs 1.5 lakh of the expenses and pay an additional Rs 1 lakh in compensation for deficiency in service.The Gujarat State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission passed the order in an appeal filed by Dayal Wadhwani, a resident of Bhat, who travelled to Singapore with four family members for a seven-day holiday.On reaching Singapore airport, the family waited for their checked-in luggage but was eventually informed that the bags had not been loaded onto their flight from Ahmedabad. They were told the luggage would arrive on the next flight that evening. However, the bags never arrived during the entire trip.With their belongings unavailable, the family had to buy clothes and other essentials, spending 4,439 Singapore dollars, equivalent to around Rs 2.2 lakh at the time.After returning to India, Wadhwani sent a legal notice to Air India. When the airline did not respond, he approached the Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in Ahmedabad, which awarded him Rs 1 lakh in compensation but rejected his claim for reimbursement of the shopping expenses. The commission reasoned that the family had brought the purchased clothes back to India and continued using them.Wadhwani challenged the decision before the state commission, arguing that the purchases had been necessitated by the airline's failure to deliver the luggage.Air India opposed the appeal, contending that the family should hand over the purchased articles to the airline if it wanted reimbursement, to prevent unjust enrichment or double benefit.The state commission rejected this argument, observing that missing baggage deprives travellers not only of essential belongings but also of items intended for their holiday.“If the luggage containing such articles does not reach the destination, a traveller is deprived not only of essential belongings but also of articles intended for enjoyment and recreation. Consequently, the non-availability of such articles can materially affect the traveller’s ability to enjoy the holiday as planned,” it observed.The commission said purchases made under such circumstances could not be treated as ordinary holiday shopping, as travellers might not get items in their preferred colour, size, design or style. It added that the unexpected expenditure could also reduce the money available for planned activities such as sightseeing and recreation.While allowing reimbursement, the commission deducted 25% of the shopping bill because the family had continued using the clothes after returning to India. It also deducted 375 Singapore dollars already paid by Air India, bringing the reimbursement amount to Rs 1.5 lakh.The airline was additionally directed to pay Rs 1 lakh in compensation for deficiency in service.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Ahmedabad | Silver Rate in Ahmedabad | Bank Holidays in Ahmedabad | Public Holidays in Ahmedabad | Ahmedabad AQI | Weather in Ahmedabad | Petrol Price in Ahmedabad | Diesel Price in Ahmedabad | CNG Price in Ahmedabad | LPG Price in AhmedabadStay updated with the latest Ahmedabad news. articles.title: Joel Kaplan, the man who built Facebook's US policy team from scratch, is leaving after 15-plus years; here's what makes his exit 'big'
articles.summary: Joel Kaplan, Meta's chief global affairs officer and Mark Zuckerberg's top Washington adviser for over a decade and a half, will leave the company next
articles.body: Joel Kaplan, Meta's chief global affairs officer and Mark Zuckerberg's top Washington adviser for over a decade and a half, will leave the company next year. Axios first reported the move, which ends a run that began in 2011, when Facebook had no real policy operation in the US capital and Kaplan was asked to build one from the ground up.The timing is what makes this exit significant. Kaplan only took the top policy job in January 2025, replacing former British deputy prime minister Nick Clegg weeks before Donald Trump's second inauguration. He was widely seen as the executive who helped Meta repair its strained relationship with Trump, and his departure leaves the company redrawing its Washington playbook just as the US midterms approach.Kaplan shaped how Meta handled regulators, Trump and its own content rulesA Harvard Law graduate and former Marine artillery officer, Kaplan was deputy White House chief of staff for policy under President George W. Bush before joining Facebook. According to Axios, he shielded Meta's personalised ads business from regulatory attacks worldwide, starting in Europe, and guided Zuckerberg through several changes of party control in Congress and the White House.Associates told Axios he pushed internally for Zuckerberg's free-expression principles to be applied consistently, even when that was unpopular. Zuckerberg said in a statement that Kaplan had "worked on virtually every tough issue Meta has faced" during his time there.His tenure had its share of friction. Kaplan faced accusations of favouring conservative interests in content decisions, a charge Meta has denied, and employees were upset when he attended Brett Kavanaugh's Supreme Court confirmation hearing in 2018.Meta is splitting Kaplan's job between four executivesKaplan will stay through the midterms and into 2027 to oversee a handover that spreads his responsibilities across executives with ties to both parties. Dina Powell McCormick, Meta's president and vice chairman, will add external affairs to a portfolio that already includes co-heading Meta Compute, the company's AI infrastructure initiative.Chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney, a former Trump trade official and ex-Microsoft general counsel, picks up policy duties. He recently led Meta's teen safety settlement with 52 US state and territory attorneys general. Brian Rice, once an aide to former Secretary of State John Kerry, was promoted earlier this year to head US government affairs. Tucker Bounds, a former spokesman for the late Senator John McCain and a Meta veteran of more than a dozen years, was named global head of communications and public affairs last month.The reshuffle comes as Zuckerberg's own focus shifts to AI. Axios reports he has moved his desk to work alongside the teams building Meta's Muse models, including its first frontier model, Muse Wonder. With data centres and AI now topping the agenda, the policy battles ahead look very different from the ones Kaplan walked into in 2011.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Mark Zuckerberg’s wife Priscilla Chan, who gave $1.48 million to a Hawaii hospital through Chan Zuckerberg Initiative; on 10 years of association with the island community: What began as a desire to ...
articles.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have donated $1.48 million to Hawaii’s Wilcox Medical Center, the latest contribution in what Chan
articles.body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan have donated $1.48 million to Hawaii’s Wilcox Medical Center, the latest contribution in what Chan described as a 10-year philanthropic relationship with the island community of Kauaʻi. The donation was made via the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and will help fund a mobile MRI unit and a new 3D mammography machine at Wilcox Medical Center, according to Hawaii Pacific Health. The gift comes as Chan reflects on a decade of philanthropy in Kauaʻi. In a message published by the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, Chan said, “What began as a desire to give back to a place we call home has grown into lasting partnerships with organizations dedicated to strengthening communities, caring for local families, and stewarding the people and places that make Kauaʻi so special.According to the initiative, 2026 marks 10 years of philanthropic work on Kauaʻi, with more than $100 million committed to over 100 local organisations and more than $57 million invested directly on the island.Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan funding healthcare infrastructureWilcox Medical Center said the $1.48 million donation will support two key imaging projects. The donation made by Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan will pay for a MRI unit and a new 3D mammography machine. The mobile unit for MRI will work as a stopgap while the hospital renovates its existing MRI suite which is said to complete in coming eight months. For the uninitiated, Wilcox performs more than 4,000 MRI scans a year, and the temporary unit will keep those exams available during the work. The 3D mammography unit, along with the room renovations needed to install it, will support breast cancer screening. Wilcox says it was the first medical center on Kauaʻi to offer 3D mammograms, in 2010, and it performed more than 8,500 mammograms last year. The hospital notes that the clearer 3D images are especially valuable in Hawaiʻi, where many women have dense breast tissue.Wilcox CEO Jen Chahanovich said the couple has repeatedly stepped forward to make sure the community has access to the best medical technology.More than $4 million donated to Wilcox by Chan Zuckerberg InitiativeAccording to Hawaii Pacific Health, the latest contribution is the couple’s second donation specifically aimed at expanding imaging technology at the hospital. Chan, a paediatrician, and Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, have now made five contributions to Wilcox programmes and services totalling more than $4 million.Previous donations have supported telemedicine initiatives, Covid-19 relief efforts, and renovations of the Wilcox Emergency Department and Trauma Center.Health care the biggest focusHealth and wellbeing is the largest area of investment. It includes a $10 million commitment to the University of Hawaiʻi medical school’s Kauaʻi Medical Training Track, which offers full tuition scholarships to future physicians who agree to practice on the island after residency. The program has 22 doctors in training and has graduated its first cohort of five. Support has also gone to a new CT scanner at Wilcox, urgent care expansion on the North Shore, and mental health services for families.Housing, schools and local jobsBeyond health, the couple’s giving has covered affordable housing, which accounts for nearly a quarter of the total, along with education and youth, food production and distribution, workforce development, cultural lands and emergency relief. Most grants from the Chan Zuckerberg Kauaʻi Community Fund of the Hawaiʻi Community Foundation are unrestricted, so nonprofits can decide how to spend them. Koʻolau Ranch, the couple’s island home, has created 189 local jobs, the initiative said.‘Meaningful giving begins with listening’In her message marking the decade-long milestone, Chan said the family’s approach has been shaped by conversations with residents, community leaders and service providers. “Throughout the past ten years, we’ve learned that meaningful giving begins with listening,” she wrote.The Chan Zuckerberg Initiative said its Kauaʻi philanthropy has supported 101 organisations through 296 grants, focusing on areas including health and wellbeing, affordable housing, education, workforce development, food security and emergency relief.Chan added that the chance to learn from, volunteer with and build relationships across the community had been “one of the greatest gifts of this journey.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Olivia Wilde sells her Studio City home in Los Angeles for $5.23 million, nearly $700,000 less than the $5.9 million she paid in 2023
articles.summary: Olivia Wilde has sold her Studio City home in Los Angeles for $5.23 million, almost $700,000 below the $5.9 million she paid in March 2023.
articles.body: Olivia Wilde has sold her Studio City home in Los Angeles for $5.23 million, almost $700,000 below the $5.9 million she paid in March 2023. The four-bedroom house closed on 2 December, less than three months after it was listed at $6.2 million. The sale comes as the actress and director's relationship with the British art dealer Caspar Jopling draws attention, and as she is reported to be considering a move to the United Kingdom. Below, you will find the price history, the property's features, the timing of the sale, the relationship context and her earlier Silver Lake house sale.Olivia Wilde sold her Studio City house for $5.23 million, beneath the $5.9 million she paid in 2023Property records cited by Realtor show that Olivia Wilde sold her Studio City house on 2 December for $5.23 million. She had bought the four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom property for $5.9 million in March 2023, so she held it for less than three years and sold it for nearly $700,000 less than she paid. Wilde had listed the house for $6.2 million less than three months before the sale closed, which puts the final price about $970,000 below the asking figure. Put another way, she accepted $5.23 million for a property she had priced at $6.2 million less than three months earlier. The house was listed through Compass, which marketed it on the strength of its architectural pedigree, layered detail and indoor-outdoor flow.Inside the 3,700 square foot house on a 0.66 acre lot with pool, spa, guesthouse and outdoor kitchenThe house was originally designed by Barbara Bestor and completed in 1940, and it underwent an extensive refresh in 2015. The Richest reported that the renovation modernised the layout, finishes and interior elements while preserving the original structure. The property covers 3,700 square feet on a 0.66-acre lot, where mature trees and structured landscaping provide privacy from neighbouring homes. Inside, an open floor plan brings together a chef's kitchen, a living area and a dining room. Wide glass doors connect the primary bedroom directly to a backyard with a pool, spa, fireplace and detached guesthouse, and a large patio also includes an outdoor kitchen. A porte cochère leads to the garage area and gives covered access to the side of the house.Caspar Jopling, July 2025 and sightings in London and New York, why a move abroad is being discussedWilde has been dating the British art dealer Caspar Jopling, 33, since July 2025, around a year after his split from the singer Ellie Goulding. The couple were photographed strolling through Primrose Hill in London in October and in New York the following month, but they have not been seen together in public in Los Angeles, where Wilde has been based for many years. Insiders told Realtor that Wilde is considering a move across the Atlantic, and the report notes she has been spending a good deal of time in Jopling's native United Kingdom. Her romance with the singer and actor Harry Styles had ended shortly before she bought the Studio City house in March 2023. Wilde has not yet commented on the relationship, so any relocation remains unconfirmed.Silver Lake house sold for $4.2 million off-market in the same month the custody terms were finalisedThe Richest reported that the Silver Lake house Wilde previously co-owned with Jason Sudeikis sold off-market in September 2023 for $4.2 million, later that year after she bought the Studio City property. The couple finalised their custody arrangement the same month. It provides for equal weekly parenting time and requires Sudeikis to pay $27,500 a month in child support. They share a son, Otis, 11, and a daughter, Daisy, 9. Wilde is 41, and Sudeikis is 50. When they ended their seven-year engagement in 2020, Wilde took the California properties, and Sudeikis kept the Brooklyn townhouse they had previously owned together. Wilde bought the Studio City house in March 2023, so the Silver Lake sale and the custody settlement both fell within a few months of that purchase.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision?
