articles.title: Meet Dev Rai, the Indian-American Virginia student who founded a nonprofit at 15 to help artisans in India; two years later, it has supported over 400 craftspeople, sold 900 products and mobilised 300 volunteers
articles.summary: At 15, while many teenagers are focused on school and extracurricular activities, Dev Rai established a nonprofit to help traditional artisans in India
articles.body: At 15, while many teenagers are focused on school and extracurricular activities, Dev Rai established a nonprofit to help traditional artisans in India reach more customers. Two years later, his initiative, Serving Society Global Foundation, has raised more than $15,000, supported over 400 artisans, sold more than 900 handcrafted products and mobilised over 300 young volunteers. According to the organisation’s official website, its work combines support for economically disadvantaged communities with environmental sustainability and cultural preservation. Based in Virginia, the initiative connects Indian craft traditions with American buyers, while giving young volunteers opportunities to develop leadership, business and communication skills.How a visit to India inspired the initiativeRai, an Indian-American student at Oakton High School in Virginia, founded Serving Society Global Foundation in 2024. The idea emerged from his visits to India, where he encountered artisans producing intricate handmade goods but struggling to secure consistent access to markets and recognition for their work. In an interview with FFXnow published on August 10, 2026, Rai explained that he saw an opportunity to introduce these products to American communities. He wanted to combine his interest in entrepreneurship and storytelling with his appreciation for Indian art and his desire to create a measurable social impact.Rather than starting from scratch, Rai reached out to nonprofit and government-supported organisations in India that were already working with artisans. These partnerships helped the foundation source handcrafted products and bring them to buyers in the United States.Connecting artisans with American buyersServing Society focuses on helping artisans gain exposure beyond their immediate markets. Its products are introduced to customers through temples, cultural festivals, community events, grocery stores and other partner locations. The foundation’s official website reports that it has raised more than $15,000 for over 400 marginalised artisans and sold more than 900 items through eight local partner locations. The products include culturally inspired goods and environmentally conscious items, allowing the organisation to promote traditional craftsmanship while encouraging more sustainable consumption.The initiative aims to do more than sell individual products. By creating a route to American customers, it seeks to help artisan communities generate income and bring greater visibility to skills and designs passed down through generations. The foundation also supports the promotion of underrepresented cultures. Its model brings handmade products into everyday community spaces, giving customers opportunities to discover the people and traditions behind them.Mobilising young volunteers across statesOne of the initiative’s most significant developments has been its expansion among students. What began as a small project has grown into a network with seven chapters, 18 youth leaders and more than 300 volunteers, according to the foundation and FFXnow. Many volunteers are associated with the SEWA DC Youth Group. Students have helped with product sales, events and outreach, while social media and networking have helped the organisation attract participants beyond its original local base. Young people from Maryland, New Jersey, Minnesota and other parts of Virginia have expressed interest in establishing or leading chapters.Rai told FFXnow that he was surprised by how readily other students took ownership of the mission. Volunteers have progressed from helping at events to proposing ideas and leading activities of their own. The experience has also shaped his approach to leadership. Instead of managing every task himself, he has learned to delegate responsibilities and create opportunities for others to contribute.Balancing school with nonprofit workRunning a growing organisation while attending high school requires careful planning. Rai told FFXnow that he tries to complete many projects during the summer, when students have fewer academic commitments. During the school year, he prioritises urgent tasks, breaks larger projects into weekly goals and plans around school deadlines. Delegation has become an important part of keeping the foundation's work manageable and sustainable.The organisation also provides volunteers with practical experience in business, communication and leadership. By helping organise events and connect products with customers, students can learn how a community-focused initiative operates while contributing to a wider social goal.Aiming for greater independence for artisansThe foundation’s future plans extend beyond selling products on behalf of artisan groups. Rai wants to help these communities build their own digital infrastructure so they can showcase, market and sell their work directly to customers. The aim is to reduce reliance on intermediaries and give artisan organisations tools they can continue managing independently. Such systems could help them reach wider audiences while maintaining greater control over how their products are presented and sold.For Rai, the longer-term goal is also to build an organisation that continues developing young leaders, even after its founder and early volunteers move on from school. Serving Society Global Foundation illustrates how a student-led initiative can connect cultural preservation, entrepreneurship and community service. Its progress so far reflects both the demand for traditional handmade products and the willingness of young volunteers to contribute to a cause beyond their own communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Missing German WW2 U-boat discovered off Devon 82 years on
articles.summary: The U-672 sub was identified 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe after divers discovered it in August.
articles.body:
A German submarine that went missing during World War Two after being damaged by the Royal Navy has been discovered 82 years on.

Plymouth dive team Gasperados identified the U-672 about 20 miles (32km) off Salcombe, Devon, after it was discovered by a deep sea diving team from Portland in August at a depth of about 230ft (70m).

The vessel was attacked by HMS Balfour in July 1944 but was scuttled by its 52 crew - all of whom survived. A navy log showing the sinking had incorrect coordinates, resulting in it not being found until recently.

Members of Gasperados said they were "really pleased" they could help identify the vessel.

Gasperados diver Dominic Robinson said: "Once we started moving around it and I started seeing the individual features - I saw the snorkel, I saw the conning tower, all those kind of things - I knew that we were going to get the video needed to identify it, so I was really pleased about that."

After its attack, the U-boat was left leaking underwater.

Its commander waited for as long as possible before making the decision to blow the tanks and bring the sub up to give its crew a last chance of survival.

Robinson said they "managed to get it to the surface" before getting into their life rafts for survival.

"They were bobbing around in the sea and then the very next day they were found by British aircraft, British vessels and then taken away to the prisoner of war camp," he explained.

German World War Two historian Dr Axel Niestle, who specialises in U-boats, said the wreck "was in the correct position" but, "due to a clerical error in the documents", had a position recorded which differed "some 46 miles (74km) from the actual position".

The surviving crewmembers returned to Germany after the war, including the U-boat's skipper.

Robinson said he had spoken to his family, who said he lived a "long and happy life".

He added: "They just said how proud he would have been and how pleased he would have been to know that it had been found at last."

articles.title: A Kandinsky masterpiece stolen by the Nazis in 1940 was returned to the heirs of its Jewish owners in 2023; the 1907 painting has now sold at auction for nearly $42 million
articles.summary: A 1907 masterpiece by Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky, looted from a Dutch-Jewish family during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, sold at a London
articles.body: A 1907 masterpiece by Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky, looted from a Dutch-Jewish family during the Nazi occupation of the Netherlands, sold at a London auction earlier this week for £31.56 million (about $42 million, including fees), The New York Times reported. The painting, Das bunte Leben (The Colorful Life), was returned to the family’s heirs in 2023 after decades of disputed ownership.A Paris canvasWassily Kandinsky painted Das bunte Leben in Paris in 1907. At 130.5 × 162.6 centimetres, it was the largest canvas he had completed to that date.Christie’s describes it as a key work from his years in the city. With this painting, he wanted to “let the viewer take a stroll within the picture” and “become absorbed” in it. “In this particular case, one strolls into a mysterious panoramic landscape teeming with life,” the auction house said.Kandinsky had high hopes for Das bunte Leben. In October 1907, it was exhibited at the Salon d’Automne. German art dealer Herwarth Walden later acquired the painting and displayed it in a 1912 exhibition of Kandinsky’s work at his Berlin gallery, Galerie Der Sturm.In November 1927, Amsterdam businessman Emanuel Albert Lewenstein and his wife, Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann, bought it. The couple ran a sewing machine business in Amsterdam and built a collection that also included works by Jan Toorop and Jozef Israëls. The painting was later lent to the Stedelijk Museum, according to The Times of Israel.When Nazi Germany invaded the Netherlands in 1940, the Lewenstein collection was broken up. In October 1940, the Kandinsky was taken from the Stedelijk and sold at auction. “It remains unclear under whose direction the works came to market, or who benefited from the proceeds,” the auction house said. The painting was then bought by Dutch collector Salomon B. Slijper. After his death in 1971, it entered the collection of Bayerische Landesbank in Germany, where it hung for decades.Historians have struggled to establish exactly how the painting was sold. In 1972, German bank Bayerische Landesbank (BayernLB) purchased it and lent it to the Lenbachhaus museum in Munich, where it remained on public display.“In 1972, BayernLB legally acquired the painting ‘Das Bunte Leben’ by Kandinsky at the instigation of the City of Munich. The purchase negotiations were handled by the Lenbachhaus museum, where the painting has been publicly displayed on permanent loan ever since. Nonetheless, BayernLB is willing to take part in a review by the so-called Limbach Commission. BayernLB feels, however, that the commission’s decision should be binding on all parties. BayernLB has expressed its desire that the painting remain on public display at the Lenbachhaus rather than be taken away,” BayernLB told The Guardian in 2017.The heirs reportedly filed a lawsuit against the bank in 2017. They spent years reconstructing the painting’s history, working with their own advisers and the Mondex Corporation. In June 2023, the bank returned the work to the heirs of Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann.The London saleOn Wednesday, 14 October, Christie’s sold the painting in its 20th/21st Century London Evening Sale. It beat its pre-sale high estimate of £25 million, closing at £27 million before fees and £31.56 million with them. The masterpiece was the top seller of the evening. The identity of the buyer has not been disclosed.Christie’s describes Das bunte Leben as a painting “bursting with a kaleidoscopic play of vivid colour and vitalistic energy”. It is among the early masterworks of Kandinsky’s storied career, the auction house said.“Executed on a monumental scale that reveals the artist’s bold ambitions for the work, the canvas is alive with detail and incident, independent touches of vibrant pigment building a mosaic-like pattern that describes a panoramic, romantic view of the often conflicting and contrasting aspects of the lived experience. The scene teems with intriguing vignettes, the lively cast of characters offering juxtaposing visions of love and death, peace and chaos, danger and an idyllic, festive atmosphere, creating a rich symphonic composition that conveys the multifaceted nature of human existence,” the auction house described.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, Chance the Rapper’s charity selected a Chicago youth therapy programme for a $100,000 grant, backing three years of support including safe summer experiences for children affected by violence
articles.summary: Chance the Rapper’s philanthropic work in Chicago extended beyond education, with his nonprofit organisation SocialWorks directing funding towards mental
articles.body: Chance the Rapper’s philanthropic work in Chicago extended beyond education, with his nonprofit organisation SocialWorks directing funding towards mental health services for communities that often struggle to access care. One of its beneficiaries was Under the Rainbow, a youth therapy programme run by Sinai Health System that works with children, adolescents and their families affected by trauma and community violence. Based on reporting by SocialWorks, alongside coverage by ABC News and CBS News on Chance the Rapper’s mental health philanthropy, the programme was selected in December 2019 as one of six recipients of SocialWorks’ My State of Mind initiative, which was designed to improve access to mental health support and encourage more open conversations about emotional well-being. The grant was meant to fund services for three years, including therapeutic summer camps and activities where young people and their families could connect in a safe environment outside traditional clinical settings. Continued support was especially important because nearly 85 per cent of young people in Under the Rainbow were reported to have PTSD, and all had experienced community violence.Making mental health support more accessibleThe grant formed part of a wider commitment announced by Chance the Rapper, whose real name is Chancelor Bennett, in October 2018. Through SocialWorks, he pledged $1 million towards mental health services in Chicago, with six providers in Cook County set to receive grants of $100,000 each.As reported by ABC News and CBS News at the time, the initiative sought to address barriers to mental health care and connect residents with appropriate services. My State of Mind was developed as part of that effort, with a focus on helping people find wellness resources and making mental health support easier to navigate.The programme also reflected SocialWorks’ broader community-focused approach. Founded to empower young people through arts, education and civic engagement, the organisation has pursued projects intended to expand opportunities for Chicago residents, particularly young people from underserved communities.Under the Rainbow’s selection reflected the importance of combining professional mental health care with experiences that help families build trust and emotional connections. For children exposed to violence, support can extend beyond appointments with therapists to include environments where they can feel safe, participate in activities and connect with others facing similar challenges.Creating safe spaces beyond traditional therapyThe funding was expected to help Under the Rainbow continue offering activities such as therapeutic summer camps, giving children and families opportunities to engage in healing outside the traditional therapy room. For Sinai Health System, the partnership offered a way to sustain services for young people dealing with difficult experiences while broadening the ways they could access support. SocialWorks, meanwhile, viewed the grants as an opportunity to back organisations that were already connected to their communities and were approaching mental health care through a combination of clinical treatment and community-based programmes.The initiative highlighted a central challenge in youth mental health: access to care is not only about the availability of professional services, but also about creating environments where seeking help feels acceptable and safe.By supporting Under the Rainbow, SocialWorks aimed to help preserve a programme that addressed trauma while giving young people and their families opportunities to connect, recover and build resilience. The partnership was one part of Chance the Rapper’s wider effort to invest in Chicago communities through philanthropy, with mental health support placed alongside education and youth development as areas requiring long-term attention.You use AI every day. articles.title: Google rolls out new Gemini tools to help small businesses save time
articles.summary: Google has announced a set of new Gemini tools aimed at small business owners, led by a dedicated business landing page inside the Gemini app.
articles.body: Google has announced a set of new Gemini tools aimed at small business owners, led by a dedicated business landing page inside the Gemini app. The company says tens of millions of small business owners already use Gemini to brainstorm products, handle customer feedback and analyse performance, and that the new tools are meant to give them time back so they can focus on the work they started their companies for. The announcement was published on Google’s India blog by Vishnu Sivaji, Senior Director of the Gemini app.The landing page is designed as a central hub where owners can build their brand, analyse finances and understand customer insights. Gemini can also now connect to Google Business Profile, Google Ads and Google Workspace, as well as third-party apps including Adobe, Canva, Dropbox, Shopify, Wix, Zoho and Xero.Brand-consistent visualsBusinesses can now define their brand style in Gemini by uploading a website, brand kit, fonts or colour palettes. Paired with Nano Banana 2.1, Google’s latest image-generation model, Gemini can produce end-to-end visuals for product launches and marketing campaigns. Google says Gemini remembers the brand style, so owners do not have to upload their guidelines each time they want new on-brand material.Financial insights from messy recordsGemini can also turn disorganised spreadsheets, receipts and purchase records into clear financial graphics and interactive models within seconds, according to Google. The aim is to let owners get insights in plain language rather than working through the numbers themselves.Business owners in India and elsewhereGoogle highlighted several users to illustrate the tools. In Maharashtra, farmer and content creator Santosh Jadhav turned his traditional fields into a ginger farm with no formal training or local mentors. He used Gemini as a virtual agronomist to judge soil suitability, calculate seed requirements and draft an investment budget, and he shares his farming journey online to show how easily AI can be used in everyday agriculture.In Jakarta, Gumilang turned a neglected space under train tracks into Barelz Arena, a sports and entertainment hub. With no background in branding or sports, he used Gemini to develop a “Brazilian-street” visual identity, design merchandise and draft partnership proposals. In Bordeaux, France, ceramicist Morgane says Gemini saves her two to three hours a day by drafting product descriptions, newsletters and social media hooks. In Goiânia, Brazil, personal organiser Patricia Morais uses Gemini for customer service and content while working on accessible products such as clothing QR codes for people with visual impairments.AvailabilityThe business landing page, the new marketing and finance skills and the additional connected apps will begin rolling out in the coming days to all Gemini app users worldwide, Google said. For larger organisations that want centralised admin controls, data governance and enterprise-grade security, the company pointed to its separate Gemini for business offering.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Dubai based man paid Rs 7,000 for matrimonial services but was repeatedly sent the same unsuitable profiles; consumer commission orders platform to pay Rs 37,000
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A Kerala based consumer commission has held a matrimonial services agency guilty of unfair trade for allegedly inducing a customer to buy a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A Kerala based consumer commission has held a matrimonial services agency guilty of unfair trade for allegedly inducing a customer to buy a higher priced package by promising him personalised matchmaking assistance but eventually failing to provide the same.The Kollam District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission directed the matrimony platform and its managing director to jointly and severally refund Rs 7,000, pay Rs 20,000 as compensation and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs. It also ordered them to stop misleading the consumers with assurances of personalised assistance, in its October 9, 2026, order.Personalised matchmaking disputeAccording to the commission order, the complainant, Akhil Vinod, approached the Intimate Matrimony after seeing an online advertisement offering personalised matrimonial services. He installed its application on July 29, 2025, following which the representatives from the platform contacted him.Employed in Dubai, the complainant informed the matrimonial agency that voice calls could be made only through BOTIM, while profiles and other communications could be shared through WhatsApp. The agency accepted the arrangement and told him that its Kollam branch would provide the services.The complainant alleged that the agency promised active matchmaking and profiles suited to his preferences. Although he initially intended to purchase a basic plan costing Rs 3,000, representatives persuaded him to choose a higher priced package by promising enhanced services.He paid Rs 7,000 and alleged that he was also made to digitally sign an agreement requiring an additional Rs 15,000 if a marriage materialised through the agency.According to the complaint, the profiles shared were unsuitable. Despite requesting alternatives, the agency repeatedly sent the same profiles and eventually stopped providing meaningful assistance. The complainant alleged that repeated requests for services or a refund went unanswered, while representatives told him that suitable profiles were unavailable.The agency and its managing director appeared before the commission on April 29, 2026, but subsequently remained absent and did not file their response. The commission proceeded without their version.Commission's findingThe bench comprising president S K Sreela and member Stanly Harold held the agency guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, finding that the complainant had paid for personalised assistance that was not meaningfully provided.The commission clarified that a matrimonial agency cannot guarantee a marriage, as the outcome depends on several factors, including the preferences and consent of the people concerned. However, the dispute concerned the failure to provide the services promised in exchange for payment.It observed that repeatedly sharing unsuitable profiles despite requests for alternatives, followed by a failure to provide meaningful assistance, did not meet the agency's obligations.The commission noted that the opposite parties had produced no material explaining the services rendered or the efforts made to identify suitable profiles.“The opposite parties have produced no material explaining the services actually rendered,” the bench said.The bench held that misleading assurances followed by failure to provide the promised assistance constituted unfair trade practice.“The misleading inducement to purchase the higher plan, followed by the failure to provide the promised assistance, constitutes unfair trade practice,” it added.The commission further stressed that matrimonial agencies must clearly disclose the scope and limitations of their packages.“The mere execution of a consent form does not establish satisfactory performance of the services undertaken,” the commission further added.Final orderThe commission allowed the complaint and directed Intimate Matrimony and its managing director to:Refund Rs 7,000 jointly and severally.Pay Rs 20,000 as compensation for mental agony, harassment and inconvenience.Pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.Discontinue and not repeat the unfair trade practice of inducing consumers to buy enhanced packages through misleading assurances of personalised assistance.The monetary directions must be complied with within 45 days of receiving the order. In case of default, the compensation of Rs 20,000 will carry interest at 9 percent per annum from the expiry of that period until realisation.The total amount payable is Rs 37,000, excluding any interest arising from non-compliance.

articles.title: Doon study flags health risks from kitchen emissions, excavation dust
articles.summary: DEHRADUN: Frequent digging of roads across Dehradun for utility works, including the laying of sewer lines, water pipelines and piped natural gas lines,
articles.body: DEHRADUN: Frequent digging of roads across Dehradun for utility works, including the laying of sewer lines, water pipelines and piped natural gas lines, is adding to the city’s particulate pollution burden, with a Doon University study flagging health risks from excavation dust and restaurant kitchen emissions.Published earlier this year in the journal Environmental Monitoring and Assessment, the study, titled ‘Evaluation of particulate matter from kitchen eateries and road dust: oxidative potential and health impacts in the Himalayan foothill city, Dehradun’, recorded an average PM2.5 concentration of 301.16 micrograms per cubic metre in restaurant kitchens, while PM10 levels at road excavation sites averaged 201.16 micrograms per cubic metre.The researchers examined the particles’ chemical composition, their potential to cause cellular damage and the extent to which they could settle in different parts of the respiratory system.The study found that fine particles (PM2.5) can travel deep into the lungs, while larger particles (PM10) tend to settle in the nose, throat and upper airways. Its modelling also found that older people had the highest estimated particle deposition in the respiratory tract, while infants had the lowest.However, lower estimated deposition does not necessarily mean lower health risk, as the impact can also depend on particle composition, toxicity, exposure duration and a person’s vulnerability, the study pointed out. The researchers called for better ventilation and vented cooking stoves in eateries, along with effective dust-control measures at excavation sites.Researcher Vijay Shridhar said dust-control measures were lacking at excavation sites and residents should not have to bear the pollution caused by development work in densely populated areas.He added that particles released by burning biomass, wood and coal in eateries could have greater oxidative potential than mineral-rich road dust, even when their concentrations were lower. “There is a need for coordination among govt agencies to prevent repeated digging of the same roads for various utility services,” he said.Shridhar clarified that sampling was conducted over two hours to analyse the particles’ chemical composition and oxidative potential and was not intended to measure 24-hour air quality. “The purpose was not to measure 24-hour emissions. Even one or two hours of exposure to such pollution can affect people living in populated areas,” he said.The concerns over excavation dust come amid frequent road digging across the city for utility works. During an inspection of Chakrata Road last week, district magistrate Ashish Chauhan flagged excavation without permission and directed officials to issue a notice to the Asian Development Bank (ADB) authorities concerned. He warned that road digging must be carried out only after obtaining the required permissions.Meanwhile, PWD secretary Pankaj Pandey said a new road-cutting policy had been prepared and was awaiting state govt approval. The policy is aimed at regulating road excavation and improving coordination among agencies undertaking utility works.Stay updated with the latest Dehradun news. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: ‘I am still traumatised’: French police accused of brutalising minors
articles.summary: Police violence and use of crowd-control weapons deepen mistrust between French authorities and demonstrators.
articles.body:
Paris, France — Enzo, 17, said a police officer grabbed his arm as another struck him from behind with a baton. With his head covered in blood, he was hospitalised and needed stitches.

Eden, a 14-year-old, cannot talk right now. His jaw was smashed after a police officer fired a tear gas grenade at his face in Saint-Ouen-l’Aumone.

Mael, 16, cannot see from her right eye after being struck by a rubber-bullet launcher fired by the police.

Since mid-September, when French high school students started revolting against the education system they say has failed them, police tactics have come under scrutiny. Lawyers and protesters who spoke to Al Jazeera accused police of stirring violence and resentment, rather than seeking to de-escalate tensions.

While authorities in France have defended the police over their actions as a necessity, violence against minors will deepen the gap between the state and its citizens, experts and lawyers say.

“They are losing a generation,” said Ainoha Pascual, a lawyer at the Paris Bar. “The government is implementing a strategy of terror. Because when you maim someone, when you seriously injure someone, it means that that person, and indeed everyone around them, will not return to demonstrations.”

Demonstrations over education have morphed into a nationwide protest movement that over the weekend saw violent clashes.

In the case of Enzo, videos verified by Al Jazeera show a peaceful crowd of teachers forming a chain in front of students. Police officers break through the cordon and, while advancing, use batons and pepper spray at close range. Screams of panic fill the air.

“I am still traumatised. Instead of protecting us, they are attacking us,” Enzo said.

According to his lawyer Elsa Marcel, Eden was sitting alone on a low wall looking at his phone, a few metres from the school protest, when three police officers approached him. Videos of the incident appear to show an officer striking the teenager with a baton before another officer fired a tear-gas grenade into his face. Marcel said the shot was fired from about 1.5 metres (5 feet) away, and accused officers of leaving the boy on the ground without calling emergency services. His family has filed a complaint for attempted murder.

“Within this social movement, this is unprecedented, especially considering that these are all minors,” said Mathilde Lante, Enzo’s lawyer and member of the Collective for Legal Action (CAJ).

French authorities denied that police were engaging in repression during the high-school protests, pointing to the hundreds of law enforcement personnel who had been injured.

In early October, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said there were “no instructions for restraint” given to police officers, stressing that the use of force had to remain proportionate. In early October, the Justice Ministry instructed prosecutors to pursue a rapid and firm response to violence during the protests, including considering parents’ civil liability for actions by minors.

Meanwhile, France’s police watchdog, the IGPN, has opened 36 inquiries into alleged misconduct. Nearly 6,900 people have been placed in police custody since the start of the protests, 86 percent of them minors, Interior Ministry figures show.

Such a tough stance seems to have only galvanised the protesters.

More than half a million people took to the streets over the weekend, about 100,000 in the capital Paris alone.

“We are too young to be taken seriously; we are grown up enough to be beaten up,” was one of the slogans on repeat.

On Saturday, police fired tear gas and stun grenades well before marches started, a move that critics said set the tone for what would become a tense day.

Police blocked roads to exit the square in Paris. Only a few narrow exit routes were left for people to leave the site. That meant that thousands were stuck and compressed, leading to fainting and panic attacks.

This is what experts call “la nasse”, or kettling, a controversial tactic in which officers encircle and contain demonstrators. It has long drawn criticism from rights groups over its impact on freedom of movement and the right to protest.

Allegations of police brutality over the years

The student-led protests ended up catalysing wider grievances in a country dealing with fiscal, political and now social crises. At times, the streets of Paris have been home to violence and vandalism.

On Saturday and Sunday, as night descended, groups of young people ransacked, set on fire and looted shops in riots.

“For the past three weeks, we’ve been hearing that ‘the police kill’ or ‘the police injure people’. And then, for the past two days, we’ve been asked, ‘What is the police doing?’ A very French kind of schizophrenia,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Monday.

This is not the first time the police have come under fire.

During the “yellow vest” protests – a period of unrest that started in 2018 over diesel price hikes and morphed into a social movement in which demonstrators wore yellow vests – officers faced criticism over their use of force, with protesters suffering serious injuries from rubber bullets and stun grenades.

In June 2023, the fatal police shooting of 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk during a traffic stop in Nanterre triggered days of riots, reigniting debate over racial profiling and police violence.

Environmental activists have also accused authorities of disproportionate force, particularly during a 2023 protest against a water reservoir in Sainte-Soline, where clashes left dozens of demonstrators and police officers injured.

Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have repeatedly raised concerns about excessive force and restrictions on the right to protest.

Paolo Stuppia, a sociology lecturer at Sciences Po Paris and co-author of the book Geopolitique de la jeunesse, believes tensions between protesters and police have worsened under French President Emmanuel Macron.

“What was once reserved for the suburbs or autonomous activist groups is now being applied to everyone,” he said. “There is a climate of mistrust between protesters and police, and it is growing because police repression now affects far more people.”

Pascual, the lawyer, argued that the severity of police violence is closely linked to the use of crowd-control weapons that can cause permanent, life-changing injuries. Rubber-bullet launchers and explosive grenades have been at the centre of controversy over police tactics in the country.

“This is truly what we call ‘French-style’ crowd control – are very specific and involve the use of weapons, including weapons described as non-lethal, but which, in reality, are capable of lethal force,” she said.

Interior Minister Nunez suspended the use of stun grenades after a teenager lost his hand. But before Saturday’s marches, he said they could be used in cases of “urban violence”, adding that they were “never used when things are going well”.

On Saturday, they were used extensively.

Al Jazeera journalists at the scene saw police fire tear gas and stun grenades repeatedly, well before the march had started.

Pascual questioned whether the use of force was effective in restoring order, arguing that de-escalation could help rebuild trust between police and demonstrators.

“When you see videos of police officers deciding to put down their shields and remove their helmets, what do you see?” she asked. “The protesters opposite them stop and applaud. In France, we don’t do that.”

articles.title: Drone attack in disputed Sudan-South Sudan border region kills at least 153
articles.summary: South Sudan authorities say Sudan’s army launched drone attack on market, as MSF says it is treating 20 wounded people.
articles.body:
A drone attack on a market in Abyei, a border region disputed by South Sudan and Sudan, has killed at least 153 people, according to a South Sudanese official.

The Abyei administration’s caretaker minister of information on Tuesday blamed the attack, which took place a day earlier on Amiet Market, north of Abyei town, on Sudan’s military.

Yohanna Akol Ngor said fires continued to burn at the site and that the death toll was likely to rise.

He told the news agency Reuters that the “situation is terrible”, adding that some bodies had been burned to ashes.

Blaming the Sudanese military for the attack, South Sudan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation said drones hit several locations in the market. It said it has summoned Sudan’s ambassador and called for its northern neighbour to “refrain” from acts that endanger civilian lives and property.

There was no immediate comment from Sudan’s armed forces.

A senior Sudanese officer, who spoke anonymously to The Associated Press news agency, said the army struck fuel tankers coming from South Sudan that were headed to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

He added that those killed in the attack were RSF members and fuel smugglers, saying the military does not “target civilians”.

Unnamed diplomats told Reuters the strike hit a fuel depot in the market the RSF has used in the past to supply its fighters.

There was no immediate comment on the attack from the RSF.

In a statement on Tuesday, the United Nations secretary-general’s spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, condemned drone attacks near Amiet Market and Todach, saying dozens of civilians, including women and children, had been killed and many others injured. The statement did not identify who carried out the attacks.

The UN said many people remained missing and the death toll was likely to rise as the UN Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) continued verifying casualties.

Medical charity Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF, said it was treating more than 20 wounded people, some with severe burns.

The war between Sudan’s army and the RSF, which began in April 2023, has ignited a devastating humanitarian crisis in the country.

South Sudan says it has not taken sides, but diplomats say Abyei has become a key route for RSF fuel supplies.

Abyei is claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan, which became independent in 2011, and is jointly administered. The oil-rich region borders Sudan’s Kordofan area, which has become a major centre of fighting in the war.

articles.title: Russia frees 74-year-old American Stephen Hubbard captured in occupied Ukraine
articles.summary: Stephen Hubbard, an American imprisoned in Russia for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine, has been released as part of talks between US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
articles.body: Russia has freed Stephen Hubbard, an American who had been imprisoned in Russia for more than four years on charges of fighting as a mercenary in Ukraine following a direct plea from US President Donald Trump. Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher, was captured in occupied eastern Ukraine during Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 and accused of fighting for Kyiv in what his family and the State Department said were fabricated charges. His release was announced as US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russia’s President Vladimir Putin for talks aimed at advancing peace efforts in Ukraine. Witkoff thanked Putin for Hubbard’s release, calling Russia’s president – who is subject to an International Criminal Court arrest warrant and has clamped down on opposition at home – a “humanitarian.” A video shared with CNN showed Hubbard meeting Witkoff and Russian negotiator Kirill Dmitriev at the Pulkovo airport in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Hubbard was seen in the video standing and walking on his own. His family previously expressed concerns over his health. Witkoff told Hubbard, who had spent years in Russian prison, that Putin “sends you blessings and wishes you good things.” While Trump said the US was not required to give Russia anything in return, Hubbard’s release comes as the president faces accusations of cozying up to Moscow at the expense of Ukraine. The Trump administration’s relationship with Kyiv has been strained in recent weeks, as Ukraine accused the US of limiting intelligence sharing on incoming Russian missiles, slowing down vital Starlink services and delaying weapon supplies. Exacerbating Kyiv’s frustrations, Trump waived some sanctions against Russia last week – a move which drew bi-partisan criticism in the US. Posting on social media on Wednesday, Trump said that “out of respect for President Trump” Russia didn’t require anything in return for Hubbard’s release. But in a separate post later, he said “if sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt.” Trump said Hubbard was released after he made a request to Putin. “Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump posted. Hubbard’s son Joseph Coleman thanked Trump and other US officials for securing his father’s release. “Never once did we waver as we prayed for success in these negotiations, and we must acknowledge that this humanitarian move by President Putin in this matter is deeply appreciated,” he said. Other Americans still in Russian prisons Hubbard is the latest American to be freed from Russian detention. In August, Robert Gilman was released from Russian detention for humanitarian reasons amid severe concerns about his health. The Marine veteran was severely emaciated when he arrived back in the US on a specialized medical plane. The organization advocating on his behalf said Gilman had been tortured in Russian detention. But many other Americans remain imprisoned in Russia: This story has been updated.

articles.title: Attack on Australian MP Haines: How threats against legislators have soared
articles.summary: Abuse, threats against Australian lawmakers are rising in a country where political violence has historically been rare.
articles.body:
An Australian independent lawmaker, Helen Haines, has had both legs amputated after ⁠being struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, Victoria state, in what Prime Minister ⁠Anthony Albanese called “a deliberate attack”.

The MP’s right leg was amputated on Wednesday, two days after her left leg was amputated at a hospital in Melbourne, where the 65-year-old politician has been receiving treatment after being flown by helicopter.

“The good news in all this is that Helen is alive and she’s stable. That is the most important thing for our family,” her husband, Phil Haines, told reporters outside the Melbourne hospital.

“We are grateful and thankful that, at this stage, both her heart and her mind are in good shape,” he said.

The Australian police said it was a “targeted attack” and warned of growing “online extremism” and recorded a rise in abuse, threats and intimidation targeting lawmakers – steadily growing in a country where political violence has been rare.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has led an outpouring of support for Haines. “It’s a reminder that the world is a more dangerous and divided place than it was a generation ago,” Albanese told ABC Radio on Wednesday.

“I think that Australians do want to see their politicians be able to go about their business, to be able to get something from the back of their car, for goodness sake.”

So, why have threats against Australian lawmakers risen?

What do we know about the alleged attack?

On Monday, Haines, who entered parliament in 2019, was struck by an SUV in Wangaratta in the afternoon, sending the rural Australian town into a mix of horror and disbelief.

Haines was getting something from the boot of her car when her alleged attacker drove past in a Toyota Land Cruiser. Authorities said the 43-year-old man turned the car around before veering at Haines and pinning her against her vehicle. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the driver then reversed before ramming her again.

Police named the suspect in the attack as Brendan Nugent, who appeared in court on Wednesday but did not apply for bail or enter a plea.

He was charged with three offences: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a public official. Additional charges of cannabis cultivation and possession have also been laid against him.

Nugent will remain in custody until his next court appearance in February.

The Australian Federal Police received no warning of any imminent danger from the alleged attacker, Commissioner Krissy Barrett told reporters.

“What I can ⁠say is we didn’t have any specific intelligence that would have indicated something as atrocious as happened on Monday afternoon,” she said.

Victoria Police Chief Mike Bush said the state police could not find any direct past contact ⁠between Haines and the accused.

“Motivation is one of ⁠these things that we absolutely need to explore. His motivation for this, what we allege is a deliberate attack, is very much a centrepiece of the investigation,” Bush said.

Haines entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife, becoming known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action. She retained the rural seat of Indi in 2022 and 2025.

She was widely praised for her efforts to increase transparency in politics and crack down on corruption.

“My background in nursing guides my work. As a nurse and a midwife, you’re with people in their most joyous and difficult moments. It’s taught me that life is precious, that everyone deserves dignity and respect, that good policy starts with listening, and – as a health researcher – that facts matter,” she describes herself on her website.

“Every day, I work to be a strong, independent voice – guided by common sense, decency and a commitment to delivering for our community and your family.”

In parliament, she pushed for a national anticorruption body. She introduced a bill in 2021 for a federal integrity commission, but it was defeated.

A year later, the Australian Parliament passed the National Anti-Corruption Commission Act 2022, leading to the formation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC).

Haines, who played a major role in the passing of the bill, served as the deputy chair of the parliamentary committee on the NACC.

Why are threats against lawmakers rising?

The Australian Human Rights Commission said the attack happened “against a backdrop of increasing polarisation and threats against politicians” that could undermine democracy.

Threats against Australian lawmakers and electorate offices doubled between 2021 and 2025, with 1,067 incidents reported to police last year.

The police also charged 41 people with offences relating to threats against parliamentarians last year, after the Australian federal police formed a National Security Investigations team described by police commissioner Barrett as a “flying squad of hate disruptors”.

In the 2025 election, threats to candidates jumped 17 percent from the previous campaign.

Earlier this month, police charged three men over separate threats to politicians and government officials, and three others were sentenced by courts.

Senior opposition politician James Paterson on Wednesday called for a review of personal security in response to the alleged crime. “The reality is that Australian parliamentarians by global standards are uniquely accessible to the public and that’s a good thing,” Paterson told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

“But we can’t have a situation where shocking attacks like this take place because that will fundamentally change our democracy forever if it becomes a serious risk to your life to be a member of parliament,” he added.

Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Director-General Mike Burgess warned last year that politically motivated violence was among the agency’s fastest-growing security concerns, driven by “grievance narratives, conspiracies and online echo chambers”.

Antiterrorism police are among the agencies investigating the attack on Haines, but the police maintain that they believe it was an isolated incident and there was “no intelligence to suggest any threat to Haines”.

Nugent, a 43-year-old resident of the rural town of Tarrawingee within Haines’s electorate, has been charged with offences that carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.

The motive remains unknown, and authorities have refused to speculate while the investigation takes place.

But police said on Wednesday they were examining all possible leads, including that Nugent may have held radical antigovernment views.

“Like everyone, we’re examining social media associations, talking to witnesses, friends and colleagues,” Bush, the Victoria police commissioner, told journalists.

During the brief court appearance on Wednesday, Nugent’s lawyer said his client suffers from a rare neurological condition called idiopathic transverse myelitis and that it was his first time in custody.

Meanwhile, Wangaratta’s Mayor Irene Grant said a sombre mood has settled over the town of about 30,000 people, a regional hub about 250km (155 miles) northeast of state capital Melbourne.

“What has happened to Helen has caused the community to step back in utter disbelief. We can’t believe it; people are horrified by what has happened,” she told AFP news agency.

articles.title: Murder arrest over death of Jacqueline Causton in Zante
articles.summary: Jacqueline Causton, 66, died on the island of Zakynthos in May, an inquest hears.
articles.body:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of murdering a British woman who died in Greece earlier this year, an inquest opening has heard.

Jacqueline Causton was found unresponsive at her villa on the island of Zakynthos on 14 May, Doncaster Coroner's Court heard.

She was taken to a local hospital on the island, also known as Zante, but later pronounced dead and her body was subsequently repatriated.

Det Con Mike Tilley, of South Yorkshire Police, told the court a man had been arrested on 12 June on suspicion of murder, before being bailed and then re-arrested last weekend when "fresh evidence" emerged.

The officer said the police's probe into the case was "complex" as investigation material uncovered by the Greek authorities was "still held" in the country and that some potential witnesses were foreign nationals.

He said there was "likely to be some further pathological work" required and that the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) was yet to decide whether or not Greek or British authorities would lead the investigation.

The hearing was not told how the 66-year-old, from Bawtry in South Yorkshire, may have died.

Offering her condolences to the family, area coroner Louise Slater said the case would return to court in February 2027 for an update.

In June, Doncaster Mind paid tribute, describing Jacqueline as a "much-loved supporter" of the mental health charity.

It said she and her late husband had "brought so much joy to our community by transforming their home in Bawtry into a magical Christmas wonderland each year".

A spokesperson for the charity added: "Their kindness, generosity and community spirit touched countless lives, and we will always be grateful for everything they did to help us continue our work."

articles.title: Evacuations and shelter-in-place orders issued in Toledo, Ohio, after chemical release
articles.summary: TOLEDO, Ohio — Some Ohio residents have been ordered to evacuate because of the release of a chemical that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin, and other residents have been told to shelter in place, the city fire department said Wednesday.
articles.body: TOLEDO, Ohio — Some Ohio residents have been ordered to evacuate because of the release of a chemical that can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin, and other residents have been told to shelter in place, the city fire department said Wednesday. People within a 1-mile (1.6-kilometer) radius of the “hazardous materials release” were ordered to evacuate at about 10:50 p.m. Tuesday. The shelter-in-place order was issued for Toledo residents within a 3-mile (4.8-kilometer) radius beyond that area. Dense fog and haze hindered visibility in the city of about 265,000 people and local news stations reported smelling a plastic-like odor. “The release is ongoing, and crews continue to monitor the situation,” the Toledo Fire & Rescue Department said in a statement posted online early Wednesday. The department did not name the chemical. It said symptoms of overexposure include headache, dizziness, tiredness, nausea and vomiting. It advised residents to contact a medical professional if they believe they are having a reaction to exposure. “You can't tell fog from the release by looking, so please don't rely on how the air looks,” the department said in the news release. “If you are outside the evacuation or shelter-in-place zones and smell an unusual odor, please stay indoors, close windows and doors and turn off ventilation that draws in outside air.” Some schools were closed Wednesday and others delayed opening. One elementary school was opened to provide temporary shelter and buses were stationed to provide shelter as needed for residents.

articles.title: Obama, Harris lean into 'Gazamaxxing' as Black voters focus on America for the midterms — not the Mideast
articles.summary: Obama and Harris used recent speeches abroad to focus on Israel and the Palestinians, while Black voters at home appear more concerned with the midterms than the Middle East.
articles.body: African Americans may be more supportive of U.S. backing for Israel than we are hearing about, at least according to a recent Fox News Poll — but you wouldn’t know it from the attention-seeking antics of some of their most prominent political and cultural "leaders." Last week Barack Obama was in Northern Ireland, where — in between saluting his own regional peace-making accomplishments — the former president accused Israel of "taking" Palestine from Palestinians during the Jewish nation’s founding back in 1948, according to a report in the Jerusalem Post. Just a few days earlier, failed presidential candidate former Vice President Kamala Harris spoke at a conference in Korea, where she blasted both the current administration and her onetime boss, President Biden, for their "failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government’s horrific conduct in the war in Gaza." WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM And let’s not forget grievance and grift-master Ta-Nehisi Coates, who appeared on a recent Vanity Fair podcast where the writer partially blamed Harris’ 2024 defeat on her unwillingness to speak out more forcefully against America’s engagement in Gaza — or being someone, as he described, who "did not have the courage of [her] convictions." All three missives come, uncoincidentally, at the tail end of a midterm election cycle in which Black voters have unexpectedly emerged as potential king-makers in the Democrats’ scramble to retake Congress. The most consequential campaign right now is in Michigan — but Obama, Harris and especially Coates are clearly projecting onto the presidential contest in 2028. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is running a must-win race against his Republican challenger, former Congressman Mike Rogers. The key obstacle for El-Sayed is not Blacks — but Jews, who could very likely abandon Michigan Democrats owing to the Egyptian-American physician’s impossible-to-ignore antisemitic outbursts and alignment with Islamists. Michigan’s Jewish vote totals around 130,000, but in this Ozempic-thin race, every ballot will matter. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER And so enter Harris and Obama. There are far more Blacks in Michigan than Jews, but the former, like the latter, are beginning to tilt rightward. Black support for El-Sayed is far lower than it needs to be, with African Americans complaining they feel both overlooked by his campaign, as well as turned off by his over-emphasis on Israel, Gaza and Palestinian issues. As one Black Michigander summed up in a recent clever Rogers ad, "El-Sayed cares more about the West Bank than West Detroit." Harris was in Michigan in late September to campaign with El-Sayed and rally Black support. At least that was the plan. Instead, both Democrats devolved into displays of characteristic Kamala "word salad" that clearly did more harm than good. Now Obama will parachute into Detroit this weekend to mop up Harris’ mess, just as new ties emerge between El-Sayed's family and Egypt’s extremist Muslim Brotherhood. Obama may think he’s smart to drop Israel and Palestine into this already combustive mix, but the #gazamaxxing — by him, Harris and Coates — reveals more about their intractable out-of-touchness than actual Black concern for the Middle East. Indeed, according to the Fox News poll, African Americans were the racial group most likely to say the U.S. isn't supportive enough of Israel when asked the question along with White and Hispanic voters. That number was 25% compared with 19% for Hispanic voters and 15% for White voters. African American voters were also the least likely of the three groups to agree that America was too supportive of Israel, with 40% disagreeing as compared to White voters at 44% and Hispanic voters at 56%. The stat stands sharply against the ubiquitous notion that African Americans — owing to supposed shared experiences of injustice and oppression — organically align with the Palestinian experience. Take it from someone who’s both African American and Jewish American, such "intersectional" overreach is little more than a myth — Blacks and Palestinians have nothing in common. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Our Civil Rights struggle — the one my own father fought to help desegregate his South Texas school — succeeded precisely because of its commitment to nonviolence. As for the Palestinians, violence — whether in Gaza, Israel, the streets of New York and now most spectacularly, along the grand boulevards of Paris — is the only thing their "liberation" movement has ever known. Such statements are not Islamophobic — they’re simply facts. Obama and Harris know this — El-Sayed probably does too. But no matter identity and entitlement are what the Dems have always done best and none are more entitled than Harris, Obama and Coates. This is why all three chose to lean into Israel well beyond the critical eyes of the actual African-Americans they claim to care so much about — Obama and Harris, respectively, in Europe and Asia; the irrationally Israel-obsessed Coates fielding sycophantic, softball prompts from a fawning white host in New York. Masters at manipulating racial anxiety and white guilt, the trio were performing for white audiences too fearful of being canceled or called racist to offer any meaningful pushback. This is why their anti-Zionist screeds passed with scant consequence or criticism — because they landed, as intended, so far from Black ears. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ultimately, Kamala, Obama and Coates could have easily attacked Israel at a church or community event or in leading Black media outlets. But then they would have been jolted by the reality that African-Americans — now contending with outsized homicide numbers and roughly twice the unemployment figures of their white counterparts — have far more crucial concerns than chanting for a "Free Palestine."

articles.title: Trump promises more than $5,000 checks and Russia frees U.S. citizen: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Trump is making big promises on the campaign trail — but with strings attached.
articles.body: Trump is making big promises on the campaign trail — but with strings attached. Special envoy Steve Witkoff praises President Vladimir Putin after Russia frees a retired American teacher. And actor Christina Applegate reveals an MS misdiagnosis. Here’s what to know today. Trump keeps promising ‘goodies’ on the campaign trail — only if Republicans win It’s not just $5,000 checks President Donald Trump is promising to Americans if Republicans win the midterms. articles.title: Rafales, Sukhois, Tejas over the Ganga: IAF gears up for grand aerial display in Varanasi
articles.summary: Varanasi will host the Indian Air Force’s ‘Wings Over Ganges’ aerial display on October 25, bringing together fighter aircraft, helicopters, transport
articles.body: Varanasi will host the Indian Air Force’s ‘Wings Over Ganges’ aerial display on October 25, bringing together fighter aircraft, helicopters, transport planes and aerobatic teams for a series of performances over the Ganga as part of the service’s 94th anniversary celebrations. This is the fifth time the IAF is holding a flypast outside the national capital region. The parade and the flypast used to take place at Palam Air Force Base till 2005, then the venue changed to Hindan, in Ghaziabad in UP. The IAF Day parade still takes place at Hindan, but the flypast has moved away from NCR under the Prime Minister's directive. Varanasi is the fifth location of this grand aerial spectacle. Previously, the event has taken place in Guwahati (2025), Chennai (2024), Prayagraj (2023) and Chandigarh (2022).The event, planned at Namo Ghat, will feature nine specially named formations and displays involving aircraft from different generations of the IAF fleet. The formations will include ‘Kashi’, ‘Varun’, ‘Kedar’, ‘Hanuman’, ‘Sarnath’, ‘Omkar’, ‘Ganga’, ‘Prachand’ and ‘Dashashwamedh’. 94 aircraft will participate in the aviation programme to mark 94 years of the IAF. This will include the Su-30MKI, Rafale, Jaguar, Mirage 2000, Tejas and MiG-29, alongside helicopters such as the Light Combat Helicopter (LCH) Prachand, Advanced Light Helicopter, Apache, Chinook, Chetak and Mi-17 V5. Transport and support aircraft, including the C-17 Globemaster, C-130, C-295, AN-32, IL-76, IL-78 and P-8I of the navy will fly over the historic city.The ‘Kashi’ formation will see three Kiran aircraft fly in a V-shaped pattern, while the ‘Varun’ formation will feature Advanced Light Helicopter Mk-III aircraft. A Rafale fighter will perform a low-level display under ‘Kedar’, while the Su-30MKI will feature in the ‘Hanuman’ formation. The ‘Sarnath’ segment will showcase a vintage Harvard aircraft performing precision manoeuvres.The ‘Omkar’ formation will involve three Mi-17 V5 helicopters carrying the national flag and the IAF flag. Chetak helicopters will feature in the ‘Ganga’ formation, which is expected to include a flower-petal shower over the riverfront. In the ‘Dashashwamedh’ formation, a C-17 Globemaster will lead nine Hawk aircraft from the Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team.The Surya Kiran Aerobatic Team (SKAT) will perform coordinated aerobatic manoeuvres, including loops, barrel rolls, inverted flying and the DNA formation, using saffron, white and green smoke trails. The Sarang Helicopter Display Team will demonstrate synchronised flying and formation changes. Both teams are among the key attractions of the programme.The ‘Prachand’ formation will bring together the Su-30MKI, Rafale, Jaguar, Mirage 2000, Tejas and MiG-29 in an arrow-shaped arrangement. The indigenous Tejas fighter is also expected to feature in a solo display. Aircraft from the army and navy will also participate, highlighting coordination among the three services.The aerial programme is intended to showcase the IAF’s flying skills, operational capabilities and technological progress, while familiarising residents and young people with military aviation. Rehearsals have been held over Varanasi ahead of the main display, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi will also attend.

articles.title: Russia releases imprisoned American Stephen Hubbard
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday said Russia released imprisoned American teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom the Kremlin accused of working as a mercenary in Ukraine before sentencing him to prison in 2024. “Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The United States, out of respect…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday said Russia released imprisoned American teacher Stephen Hubbard, whom the Kremlin accused of working as a mercenary in Ukraine before sentencing him to prison in 2024.

“Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release. This major return should have taken place long ago through the Biden Administration, which got nowhere in its negotiations with the Kremlin.”

The release comes after Trump has taken various moves that benefit Russia, including striking a deal to import Russian diesel and waiving sanctions meant to isolate Moscow.

The president claimed that “numerous people” who called on him to sanction Russia “have called to apologize to President Trump in that they didn’t know that he was negotiating the release of Stephen Hubbard, a truly big and important deal for the U.S.”

“If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt,” he wrote.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff first announced Hubbard’s release during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday. Witkoff thanked the Russian leader for Hubbard’s release and told Putin that because “of you, he’s going home to his family,” The Associated Press reported.

Putin replied that Hubbard was at Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg following his release.

Trump had teased to reporters Tuesday that he spoke with Putin and asked for the Michigan teacher to be released.

Hubbard was serving a seven-year prison sentence after he was accused of signing a contract with Ukraine’s military following the Russian invasion that started the war between the two countries. Russian prosecutors claimed Hubbard fought alongside Ukrainian troops before his arrest two months into the war, prompting the Biden administration to designate Hubbard as wrongfully detained.

Trump took a second swipe at his predecessor on Truth Social , later writing that former President Biden should have “done the Hubbard release a long time ago!”

“What a difference a president makes!” he added.

Hubbard is the second American detained in Russia to have been freed in just more than two months, as critics accuse the Trump administration of benefiting Russia while threatening the U.S. relationship with Ukraine amid its nearly five-year-long war against Russia.

Trump and the Kremlin made a deal earlier this month to allow diesel into the U.S. and global marketplace amid the energy shortage instigated by the Iran war. The president followed this by waiving sanctions on Russia, which were passed by Congress in a bill named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

Both acts drew condemnation from both sides of the aisle. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the diesel deal a “ birthday gift ” to Putin and urged the U.S. not to make a “ historic mistake ” by offering Putin support.

Trump has blasted back at Zelensky, calling the Ukrainian president “not a good guy for us to deal with.”
