articles.title: Jackdaw: Will it cut energy bills and how much gas will it provide?
articles.summary: BBC Verify looks at what the Jackdaw decision means for bills, energy security and the environment.
articles.body:
The government has approved drilling at the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.

The decision - which comes after years of debate and legal challenges - will pave the way for gas to be extracted from it and used in Britain's gas network within weeks.

BBC Verify has looked at what this means for energy bills, energy security and the environment.

Where is Jackdaw and how much gas is there?

Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles (241.4km) east of Aberdeen. It is owned by Adura Energy, which is itself equally owned by the energy companies Shell and Equinor.

The owners of the site, which was first approved four years ago but subject to legal delays until now, estimate Jackdaw has around 10 million cubic metres of recoverable gas.

Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.

Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Where does Britain currently get its gas from?

Around half of the UK's natural gas comes from its existing North Sea gas fields and is pumped ashore via pipelines.

Gas imports make up the remainder. Of these, most come from Norway's North Sea gas fields via separate pipelines.

But a higher share of the UK's gas imports now come in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) compared with 20 years ago.

This is natural gas which is extracted, turned into liquid form and then transported by ship to the country which buys it, where it is turned back into gas form to be used as an energy source.

And the UK increasingly relies on shipments of LNG from the US, which accounted for a quarter of all natural gas imports in 2025 .

Will the approval of Jackdaw mean lower bills?

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has said the gas from Jackdaw "won't lower energy bills this winter".

And most energy analysts do not expect the additional gas production from Jackdaw to have a significant, direct impact on households' energy bills, either.

This is because of the way natural gas markets work. Great Britain is integrated with wider European gas markets and physically linked to the continent through undersea pipelines.

Gas prices faced by British households and businesses are effectively set at a pan-European level and determined by the price customers across Europe are prepared to pay for the energy.

People across the continent have seen their energy bills rise significantly in recent years, fuelled by the wars in Ukraine and Iran affecting gas and oil supplies.

But the additional gas being pumped into the UK's system from Jackdaw will still be relatively small, and unlikely to significantly move the European price paid by British firms and households.

"Essentially, producing more British energy doesn't necessarily mean cheaper British energy," Karl Matikonis, professor of taxation at University College Dublin, told BBC Verify.

"North Sea oil and gas are sold at market prices rather than reserved for British consumers at a discount."

However, the additional production of gas from Jackdaw could result in more corporation tax revenues for the UK government, because any profits made by the owner would be taxable.

As part of its Jackdaw announcement , the government said it was setting up a new energy wealth fund, using tax revenues from North Sea oil and gas to invest in green energy projects. It said this would "help get bills down for good in the long term" by reducing the UK's reliance on gas for electricity production.

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has previously said the tax revenue from Jackdaw "could be used to bring down energy bills" more directly by taking costs of households' bills directly.

However, both proposals depend on the future profits of the owner of Jackdaw, which cannot be forecast with certainty.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said opening the gas field would "protect hundreds of jobs" and the move has been welcomed by unions.

The owner of Jackdaw has also estimated it will help support around 500 jobs, including roles on nearby production hubs, but only 27 direct roles on the Jackdaw gas extraction platform in the North Sea.

What are the arguments for and against Jackdaw?

One of the key arguments put forward in favour of developing Jackdaw is that it would improve the UK's national energy security.

Energy experts take different views on this. Some suggest that if, for some reason, foreign LNG shipments were not able to reach the UK, having additional North Sea gas from Jackdaw available and delivered through a pipeline that the UK controls might prove valuable.

They argue that the reliability of the US as a source of energy has been put into question by Donald Trump's recent comments that he was considering banning exports of US diesel to European countries.

However, others are not convinced Jackdaw would make a significant difference to national energy security because the UK would remain heavily reliant on natural gas imports even when the field is up and running.

The enviromental impact of Jackdaw has also been a significant point of contention. Advocates argue the gas field would be beneficial because the carbon emissions arising from production from the the UK's own North Sea field will be lower than those arising from the production of US LNG.

The North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the sector, has estimated the emissions arising from the production, delivery and processing of US LNG are around three times higher than from the production of North Sea natural gas.

That is because the process of liquefying, shipping and then turning LNG back in to natural gas on arrival is extremely energy intensive, compared with pumping it ashore by a pipeline, creating higher carbon emissions.

However, NSTA estimates that Norwegian North Sea gas production - which Britain already imports by pipeline in large volumes - has a considerably lower average emissions impact than that of the UK's existing North Sea gas production.

This is because UK North Sea gas mostly comes from smaller fields and is extracted with older infrastructure and technology than those of Norway.

The owner of Jackdaw estimates the emissions intensity of its production would be lower than from older UK North Sea infrastructure - though it would still be higher than gas produced from Norwegian fields.

So the impact on the environment of the Jackdaw decision partly depends on what happens to the mix of UK gas consumption in future - and where it comes from - which is uncertain.

If additional gas production from Jackdaw displaces US LNG imports, UK-related national emissions could be lower than otherwise.

But if additional gas production from Jackdaw displaces gas imports from Norway instead then UK-related national emissions could be higher than otherwise.

It's important to bear in mind that the emissions from burning gas also greatly outweigh the emissions from producing it.

And analysts argue that if the Jackdaw decision ends up increasing the overall quantity of fossil fuels produced and consumed around the whole world then it will push up global emissions compared with what would otherwise have happened, even if UK-related emissions fell.

Jonathan Stern of the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies told BBC Verify: "If what matters is global rather than UK-related emissions then any new fossil fuel development will increase emissions, because the Norwegian and US gas which might replace Jackdaw will probably be developed anyway."

However, the direct impact on global emissions would still be relatively small given the size of Jackdaw relative to existing global production and consumption of fossil fuels.

articles.title: Putin is a loser. Treat him like one.
articles.summary: The right policy is to treat Putin like the loser he is.
articles.body:
Two weeks ago, Tucker Carlson made the claim to British broadcaster Jacob Rees-Mogg that Russia’s economy dwarfs Britain’s. It doesn’t. International Monetary Fund figures show Britain’s output is about $4.3 trillion and Russia’s about $2.8 trillion — 60 percent higher.

Carlson’s claim reflects a tendency by some to treat Russia and President Vladimir Putin as powerful. That feeds a faulty policy instinct: that Putin is a peer to be bargained back into the club. The record says otherwise.

He inherited a country smarting from the collapse of the Soviet empire and, after a brief hydrocarbon-fueled recovery , set it on a path of stagnation, isolation and self-inflicted decline. The invasion of Ukraine did not reverse that trajectory — it locked it in. Putin’s Russia is weaker, sicker, poorer relative to its rivals, and increasingly a vassal to Beijing.

There is little to be gained from cultivating Putin, as he has demonstrated by deploying disinformation to stoke divisions in the West, and with his support for Iran against U.S. forces and our allies’ energy infrastructure.

The right policy is to treat Putin like the loser he is.

Putin is running Russia’s resource-abundant economy into the ground. Real GDP growth since 2013 , prior to the invasion of Crimea, has been an anemic 19 percent, compared to 34 percent for America. Massive spending on the futile war against Ukraine saw GDP growth above 4 percent in 2023-2024, but that artificial boom has stalled; growth slumped to 1 percent in 2025, and forecasts for this year are worse.

Moscow plans to spend a record $200 billion on defense in 2027, about 35 percent of federal spending, while the government has doubled its 2026 deficit estimate to 3.2 percent of GDP.

The cushion is thinner, too. Oil and gas revenue fell 24 percent in 2025, to its lowest level since 2020, supplying about a quarter of federal income, against roughly half in 2014 . The liquid part of the sovereign wealth fund has plunged since before the 2022 invasion, from about $113 billion to $47 billion . With foreign markets closed, the Kremlin borrows at home with the key rate at 14 percent ; four in five regions spent more than they collected in 2025, and a record number cut healthcare spending in real terms.

Putin spent a decade building a fortress economy. Now he is strip-mining Russia’s future to fund the front.

Some of Russia’s demographic woes predate Putin , but the war has made them worse. Russia has suffered an estimated 1.4 million casualties since February 2022, including as many as 450,000 dead; the most losses for a major power since China’s during the Korean War . At least 650,000 people have fled Russia since the invasion, and Bloomberg estimates that the economy is short of at least 1.5 million workers .

Meanwhile, life expectancy in Putin’s Russia is more than eight years less than in Europe, and the Kremlin’s own spokesman has described the low birth rate as “catastrophic for the future of the nation.”

In February 2022, the general assumption was that Russia, with an economy roughly 10 times larger , population 3.5 times larger and land mass 28 times larger , would defeat Ukraine in short order. Yet Putin’s army was humiliated in 2022 and has barely advanced since. In 2023-2025, Russia gained less than 1.5 percent of Ukraine’s territory and has hardly advanced in 2026. Russia’s Black Sea fleet has lost ships and freedom of action , and Ukrainian strikes now reach refineries deep inside Russia .

Meanwhile, Finland and Sweden have joined NATO , and Europe is rearming. Unable to break Ukraine’s army, Putin is turning on its civilians and its economy. July was the deadliest month for Ukrainians since May 2022, with homes, schools and the electricity grid among the targets.

His recent provocations toward Europe, from drone incursions to sabotage and the harassment of NATO ships and aircraft that NATO attributes to Moscow, are not the mark of a statesman extending his influence, but the desperate jabs of a leader who cannot afford a real fight.

Putin’s mismanagement and costly war of attrition is making Russia a vassal of its former rival, China. Beijing now supplies roughly 35 percent of Russia’s imports and takes 30 percent of its exports while Russia accounts for under 4 percent of China’s trade. Cut off from Western suppliers, Russia buys roughly 90 percent of its sanctioned high-tech imports from China, and its liquid sovereign wealth reserves are held in yuan and gold rather than dollars or euros.

The leverage shows up in price. China reportedly pays about 39 percent less for Russian gas than Gazprom’s other customers in foreign markets. Beijing has also reportedly pressed for gas through the proposed Power of Siberia-2 pipeline to be priced near Russia’s domestic rate. This has deadlocked a project that the Kremlin needs far more than Xi does.

Treating Putin like a loser does not mean underestimating him. Putin may well outlast his country’s decline. That is the case for deterrence, not concessions. Russia is not a peer to be courted but a declining, dangerous power to be contained.

Every month the West keeps up the pressure, the bill for Putin’s war grows — a bill he cannot pay without Beijing and cannot escape by being invited back into the club.

Ludovic Hood, a former U.S. diplomat with experience in the Middle East and Europe, is a senior fellow with the Hudson Institute’s Center for Peace and Security in the Middle East.

articles.title: Who is Stephen Hubbard, imprisoned American released by Russia?
articles.summary: Russia on Wednesday released American teacher Stephen Hubbard, who was serving a seven-year prison sentence after prosecutors accused him of working with Ukraine as a mercenary following the Russian invasion that launched the war between both countries. President Trump announced the development on Truth Social after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Hubbard was released…
articles.body:
Russia on Wednesday released American teacher Stephen Hubbard, who was serving a seven-year prison sentence after prosecutors accused him of working with Ukraine as a mercenary following the Russian invasion that launched the war between both countries.

President Trump announced the development on Truth Social after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said Hubbard was released during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Witkoff thanked the Russian president, saying Hubbard could now return home to his family.

“The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia,” Trump wrote. “There was no “swap” necessary for this release.”

The retired educator grew up in Big Rapids, Mich., and served in the U.S. Air Force and National Guard, The New York Times reported in 2025, citing military records.

Hubbard lived in Japan and then Cyprus for several years before moving to Izyum, Ukraine, in 2014, his sister Patricia Hubbard Fox told Reuters , adding that she last spoke with her brother in September 2021.

Russian prosecutors alleged that Hubbard signed a contract with the Ukrainian military at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022 and that he fought alongside Ukrainian troops. State media claimed Hubbard manned a Ukrainian military checkpoint at the start of the war, Reuters reported.

Two months after Russia’s invasion, he was captured and brought to trial. The Biden administration designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.

Russian prosecutors accused Hubbard of being part of a Ukrainian territorial defense unit and that he received training, weapons and ammunition and was told he would receive $1,000 a month, according to Reuters.

Hubbard’s lawyer, Martin De Luca, told the news service that the charges were false and that he had no involvement with Ukraine’s military and was detained at a house in Izyum. Ukrainian forces reclaimed the city in September 2022

Before Hubbard was sentenced, Russian state media claimed that he pleaded guilty to the charges.

Fox told Reuters that her brother held pro-Russian views and was not likely to take up arms at his age, and questioned the reported guilty plea.

Second release of an imprisoned American

Hubbard’s release comes after Russia released American teacher Marc Fogel in February. Fogel had been serving a 14-year sentence in a penal colony after he was convicted of allegedly trying to enter Russia while carrying medical marijuana in 2021.

The Biden-era State Department also labeled Fogel as wrongfully detained.

Fogel’s sister said that it felt like the family was “stabbed in the back” when he was not part of an earlier massive prisoner swap involving the U.S., Turkey, Germany, Russia, Poland, Slovenia, Norway and Belarus.

It was the largest exchange of detainees since the Cold War, with journalist Evan Gershkovich among those released .

National security adviser Mike Waltz said at the time that Fogel’s release “serves as a show of good faith from the Russians and a sign we are moving in the right direction to end the brutal and terrible war in Ukraine.”

articles.title: Trump: Implementing Russia sanctions would have halted Stephen Hubbard release talks
articles.summary: President Trump defended his waiver of Russian sanctions, saying it would have halted negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin regarding the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher who was arrested by Russian authorities when it invaded Ukraine. “Numerous people, who requested that sanctions be immediately imposed on Russia, have called to apologize to President…
articles.body:
President Trump defended his waiver of Russian sanctions, saying it would have halted negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin regarding the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher who was arrested by Russian authorities when it invaded Ukraine.

“Numerous people, who requested that sanctions be immediately imposed on Russia, have called to apologize to President Trump in that they didn’t know that he was negotiating the release of Stephen Hubbard, a truly big and important deal for the U.S,” Trump wrote on Truth Social .

“If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt,” he added.

Hubbard was released on Wednesday morning, according to another post by Trump. The president described making a request to Putin “in a telephone conversation last week.”

“The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release,” Trump stated.

Hubbard was serving a seven-year prison sentence after he was accused of signing a contract with Ukraine’s military following the Russian invasion that started the war between the two countries in 2022.

At his trial, Russian prosecutors claimed Hubbard fought alongside Ukrainian troops before his arrest two months into the war, prompting the Biden administration’s State Department to designate Hubbard as “wrongfully detained.”

Hubbard’s release comes after Trump faced major criticism from his own party concerning his decision to import Russian diesel amid rising global energy costs and waive a legislative package that would have imposed Russian energy sanctions.

Trump also recently negotiated a deal with Moscow to “immediately” supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the global marketplace, with another 500,000 tons on the way in November despite embargoes and sanctions.

A bipartisan group of senators — including Republican Sens. Thom Tillis (N.C.), Lisa Murkowski (Alaska), and Susan Collins (Maine) — signed onto a letter that condemned the deal, writing that lifting sanctions on Russia’s diesel exports “only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians.”

articles.title: France’s Macron says protesters won’t be allowed to ‘cause chaos’
articles.summary: French president criticises comments by ‘foreign leaders’ trying to exploit disorder for their own political agenda.
articles.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron has said people who plan to “cause chaos” during protests against the high cost of living will not be allowed to do so.

Speaking to the press in Doha, where he met Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, Macron said he would meet with French intelligence services before protests planned for Saturday.

He maintained that there has not been any “visible ‌foreign interference in the events ‌that took place”, but warned that “there had been foreign manipulation of information in the aftermath.”

More than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday to demand better conditions in schools and denounce high living costs. At least 2,500 people were arrested after riots broke out in certain areas, with shops looted.

Macron insisted he would “adopt all the measures necessary” to restore what he described as “calm, security and order”.

The French president also criticised “unacceptable and even stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders”.

Macron said the leaders were weighing in on protests in France to rally their political supporters. His comments appeared to be related to United States President Donald Trump, who claimed the protests were about immigration.

Macron’s criticism also appeared to relate to claims made by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who said France had been engulfed by an “invasion of extremist Islam”. Neither Trump nor Netanyahu provided any evidence to support their claims.

On Wednesday, France’s Yellow Vest movement filed plans for a large protest in Paris this weekend, following a second consecutive night of curfews that passed without major incidents.

Macron said it was not currently necessary to enforce a state of emergency, but Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has pledged to increase security at future protests. Lecornu said there would be a “massive deployment” of police, backed by the military.
